House again in committee on Bill No. 43, to amend the Canada Temperance Act, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Importation of intoxicating liquor prohibited:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
An amendment has
been moved that paragraphs (c) and (d) of subsection 2 of section 1 be struck out and the following two paragraphs be added as paragraphs (c) and (d) respectively:
(c)	The importation of intoxicating liquor into a province by any person duly licensed by the government of Canada to carry on the business or trade of a distiller, where the intoxicating liquor so imported is imported solely for the purpose of being used for blending with or flavouring the products of the business or trade of a distiller carried on by him in the province and while kept by him in the province is kept in a place or warehouse which conforms in all respects to the requirements of the law governing such places or warehouses and is used solely for blending with or flavouring the products of his said business or trade as a distiller; or
(d)	The importation of intoxicating liquor into a province by a person engaged in and carrying on the business of exporting intoxicating liquor from that province, where the intoxicating liquor so imported is imported solely for the purpose of his export business and while kept by him in the province, is kept in a liquor warehouse which conforms in all respects to the requirements of the law governing such ware-nouses, and when sold or disposed of by him is actually exported from that province:

The bill before
he committee consists of a single section the adoption of which carries the bill; and the amendment that has been moved will in effect put into force in British Columbia what is known as the Doherty Act without consulting the electors of the province. The provisions of that act will affect everybody in British Columbia except the liquor commission, or as that body is more properly described, in British Columbia the Liquor Control Board-control is the main object out there. Subsection (1) of section 1 is a "bone-dry" section except so far as the Liquor Control Board is concerned, and as a resident of British Columbia I protest against this legislation, as I am sure the great majority of the people of that province would protest against it if the question were submitted to them. Public opinion in British Columbia is decidedly against this legislation; I believe it is as totally averse to depriving individuals of the right to import for their own use, as it is to allowing private individuals to sell liquor in the province. And that opinion against any attempt to deprive private persons of the right to import liquor into the province is all the stronger after the people have observed the administration of the act under the Liquor Control Board during the past few years. I think that right of private individuals should be more jealously guarded. The Liquor Control Board is virtually the Attorney General of the province. The members of the board are mere figureheads; the Attorney General pulls the strings and they dance to his music. This legislation, is an infringement of public and private rights, rights which the people have never voted to have taken from them. It is not necessary in the interests of temperance, it is not necessary in the interests of moderation, to deprive the individual in British Columbia of the right to import liquor; nor is it needed to prevent that illicit sale, known as "bootlegging." This legislation is absolutely unnecessary for that purpose. To pretend that it is needed is merely to say what cannot be substantiated; any assertion of the kind is sheer pretence, a sham, a camouflage. I say, therefore, that if it is wise or fair or good legislation to allow the Attorney General of British Columbia by order in
Canada Temperance Act

council to abolish the existing subsections (c) and (d), which constitute an exception to the bone-dry section 1, and to do so without consulting the wishes of the people of British Columbia, it is just as fair and wise to allow him to nullify the two other exceptions which allow the distillers to import for purposes of their business, and common carriers to convey liquor through the province. This legislation does not allow the Attorney General to nullify these two provisions, but it gives him power by order in council to do away with the provisions of paragraphs (c) and (d). It is just as reasonable to clothe the Attorney General with the same power in regard to all four exceptions as it is to allow him to exercise the power with reference to two of them without consulting the wishes of the people. To be consistent, why not give him power to alter the whole liquor system of the province of British Columbia by order in council? Why not allow him to nullify provisions (a) and (b), one of which allows importation into the province by the provincial government, while the other provides for the carriage of liquor through the province by common carriers? Why not give him the right to abolish these provisions at his will? It is manifestly unfair to let him interfere with either set of these provisions by order in council. This parliament has no mandate to confer any such power on the Attorney General of British Columbia. The provincial government and the Attorney General of the province have no mandate from the electors of the province to legislate them out of their present rights. Why therefore should this parliament at this time infringe upon those rights? What is the excuse, what is the neces sity for it? Why clothe the attorney general with this extraordinary power?
In a prohibition province there must be a plebiscite before the Dominion government will apply the provisions of the Doherty Act. So why not a plebiscite for British Columbia, where there is much less likelihood of the people desiring what is virtually the Doherty Act than there is in the bone dry provinces. The Prohibition Act of British Columbia, which was administered most unsatisfactorily for a number of years, recognized the right of the private individual to import for export under license and for personal use. The Liquor Control Act under which we are now operating in British Columbia recognizes that right. The provincial government has never gone to the country either by plebiscite or referendum seeking the powers proposed to be conferred on them by this bill In effect the Minister of Justice is asking parliament to take away fMr. George Black.]
from the people of British Columbia rights which they did not give up and which there is no good reason why they should be deprived of at this time. Why not consult the people of British Columbia on this proposal, as was done when the plebiscite was taken in 1920, before depriving them of their undoubted constitutional rights?
To illustrate w'hat I have said, in the 1920 plebiscite the questions put to the electors were two, and I do not think anyone can read into those questions and the answers to them any excuse for this legislation. The first question was: Are you in favour of continuing the present prohibition act? The second question was:	Are you in favour of government control and sale of liquor in sealed packages? The answer to the first question was overwhelmingly "no", they did not want to continue the prohibition act; the answer to the second question was overwhelmingly "yes"; and the legislature legislated accordingly. There is absolutely nothing in these questions and answers authorizing the enactment of thfe legislation which the Minister of Justice now asks this House to pass.
I think it is an admitted fact that in a great measure the dissatisfaction prevailing in the United States to-day with regard to prohibition is because of the unfair way in which prohibition was put upon the people. They were not consulted, their rights were legislated away from them. And that is what we are trying to do to-day-to take away from the people of Britsh Columbia rights which they have never asked to be divested of. I cannot bring myself to believe that the Minister of Justice understood the conditions in British Columbia when he introduced this legislation or he would not seek to treat the people there so unfairly. There is no intimation from the people of British Columbia that they want this legislation. Why not be fair to them, why not give them a chance to say whether or not they want it? Are the people of British Columbia not to be trusted in regard to this question? Is their wish to be thrust aside to suit the whim of the Attorney General of vhat province to enhance his power? For that is all it amounts to. The Attorney General of British Columbia in asking for this legislation does not want moderation, he does not want prohibition: he simply wants power-power which the electorate of that province have never signified they wish him to be clothed with, and he has come to this parliament in this roundabout way to get this power over the heads of the people.
Hon. members opposite, particularly the right hon. Prime Minister, not so very long ago were prone to declaim against what they

Canada Temperance Act
termed "government by order in council''. When they were in opposition, less than two years ago, we heard a great deal against so-called government by order in council. Was there ever a. more flagrant case of government by order in council than that sought to be created by this bill? The situation is this: There is legislation in operation in British Columbia regulating the liquor traffic, legislation passed and put in operation at the instance of the people of that province. Now, without consulting the people of the province, it is sought by this bill to empower the Attorney General of British Columbia by order in council, to completely change the effect of the liquor legislation now in operation in that province. If that is not government by order in council, then there never was an instance of it. It is government by order in council not only of the province but of the federal government; it is distinctly order in council government. I say we should not do it. I say the Minister of Justice should not ask the House to do it. I go further, I say it is the duty of the Minister of Justice to oppose the passage of legislation of this character. It is his duty to prevent it. It is not democratic, it is not fair to the people affected.
Now, what is the excuse for this extraordinary act on the part of the government? The ordinary excuse for government by order in council of recent times has been that there was a war on, or that the government was under the stress of re-establishment. Why this extraordinary measure now with no extraordinary circumstances to excuse it? It may be said there is a war on -a war against the bootleggers of British Columbia. But I tell this House that it is only a sham fight; there is no real war on there; and it is not necessary to enforce the present liquor law of British Columbia that this bill should be enacted.
Is the Attorney General of British Columbia, is the Liquor Control Board of that province, encouraging moderation in the use of liquor? I say, no

notoriously no. As the member for New Westminster (Mr. Mc-Quarrie) said yesterday, so far as temperance goes in British Columbia "There is nothing doing in that quarter;" that is, in the vicinity of the Liquor Control Board and the Attorney General's office. What is happening? The Attorney General and the Liquor Control Board of British Columbia are actually booming the liquor trade, they are urging people to buy liquor and to drink it. Then they talk about wanting to enforce the liquor law! It was expected when this act was
put in force in British Columbia that the government there would encourage moderation in the consumption of liquor. The old crusade against the bar had its merits and had its success in the fact that the bars tempted people to drink. The idea of the true moderationists in dealing with the bar was to remove this temptation, and they expected that by the government taking over the control and sale of liquor good liquor would be made available to the people in moderate quantities at moderate prices. They never contemplated that the Lipuor Control Board should by a campaign of liquor advertising flaunt their favoured brands in flaring advertisements before the public throughout that province as they are doing to-day. Why, you would think there was a Victory bond sale going on out there, from the way the Liquor Control Board are advertising different brands of liquor. Every billboard in the country is filled up with that kind of advertising, to say nothing of newspapers-and yet they talk about moderation. The moderationists of British Columbia never supposed that there would be competition between Government liquor shops as there actually is to-day. Can you imagine competition for trade between vendors in the respective government liquor shops? Can you imagine them persuading people to buy at their particular shop so that they would mak^ records for big sales and in that way curry favour with their employers? Is that moderation? That is the sort of liquor board that this House is asked to encourage and give more power to. I say they are not fit to be entrusted with that power, but apart altogether from that, I say the people of British Columbia do not want it. The people never expected this when they voted for what was called the moderation act in British Columbia. They never expected that when reputable, old, established distilling concerns from the Old Country offered their goods for sale to the British Columbia Control Board they would find it necessary, in order to make a sale, to appoint as their agents ward officers of city Liberal associations, thereby greatly increasing the price to the public. The moderationists of British Columbia, I say, did not expect that, but that is what has been done and is being done to-day, and that is one reason why this House should not force the people of British Columbia to buy liquor from such vendors exclusively.
Now, let me say a word about the price of liquor in British Columbia. The Whiskey Association of Great Britain comprises practically all the largest and best distillers in the
Canada Temperance Act

United Kingdom. They have a minimum price for export of 55 shillings per case. They will not ship for less; anything cheaper is green whiskey and not fit for use. Fifty-five shillings at 23 cents would amount to 12.65 f.o.b. United Kingdom. Freight, insurance and charges to Vancouver would amount to SI; duty on whiskey, S10 per proof gallon, 2 gallons per case at 25 under proof; duty on whiskey; duty on glass, and Dominion sales tax adds $21 per case, which makes the landed cost of the whiskey in Vancouver $34.65 a case. What does the government charge the public for that whiskey? They charge $54 a case, making a profit of $19.35 a case. Is it any wonder that the bootlegger can do business successfully in competition with prices like that? I ask the government and I ask this committee, is it fair to prevent individuals from importing for their own use when they can bring the goods in at $34.65 a case and the government charges $54? That is another sample of the way the liquor business is handled in British Columbia. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) yesterday, and the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), referred to a local wine company there, known as the California Wine Company. There is a fine old port, product of Spain, called Con-vido port, black label, white letters. This local wine company copied the label and called it "Bonvido Fine Old Port." They sold it over the counter in the government shops as fine old port, and it was proved that the material in these bottles was nothing but loganberry juice and some truck brought up in mats and casks from California. In one instance an order went in to the wine company for 55 cases and the answer was, "WTe have not any on hand, but we will make some up for the morning,"-"fine old port" made overnight! These are the people that this House would force the consumers of British Columbia to deal with. But that is not all. Let me tell the committee something about the method employed by the Liquor Control Board in handling whiskey in British Columbia. The board purchased 1,690 cases of Roderick Dhu whiskey, 1,350 cases of Royal Stuart Scotch, 1,900 cases of Balmoral Scotch and 2,000 cases of Milburn Scotch-all cheap, inferior whiskey-and other odds and ends, amounting to something over 7,000 cases. What was done with that stuff? It was so bad that they did not dare to put it on the government shelves for sale; nobody would buy it. Well, the corks were drawn and the whole was mixed with prune juice and other ingredients in a big vat. A high voltage electrical device was employed and the stuff tM'-. George Black.]
"aged" on the spot, was rebottled and sold at S3.50 a quart, at the government shops labelled, "L. C. B."-Liquor Control Board. That is the sort of stuff this legislation would compel the people of British Columbia to buy. I am sure the Minister of Justice did not realize what he was doing when he introduced this legislation. These facts were brought out before the public accounts committee of the Legislature of British Columbia. The stuff the Liquor Control Board of British Columbia sells reminds me of a story told of a certain saloon in Dawson City in the old days. It had a sawdust floor; many of them had, but in this saloon when they sold a man a glass of whiskey they handed him a whisk broom-that was to brush the sawdust off himself when he came to. Well, the Liquor Control Board of British Columbia does not even supply a whisk broom. If the Liquor Control Board handles wine and whiskey like that while people who know enough or have money enough to do so import for their own use, what will they not do when you give them the monopoly this legislation creates and force people to buy from them exclusively?
Under the law as it is at present in British Columbia the individual who imports foi his own use is taxed by the British Columbia government the amount of profit the government would have made had the government sold him the liquor, so the government loses nothing on the transaction. It is not in competition with the government, but by importing it personally the importer is sure of the quality and does not take the fearful risk of having the liquor doctored up as I have described. Do you think it is fair to prevent him from importing his own liquor when he would otherwise have to buy stuff like that? There is no bootlegging in British Columbia by private importers. Any bootlegging that is done there can easily be controlled by the Attorney General of the province with the legal machinery he already has. I leave it to the Minister of Justice or to any member of the committee: would he want to buy liquor from a dealer who does as I have described? AVould he feel safe? The Minister of Justice said yesterday that the reason for this legislation was a desire.to stop bootlegging. I can tell him and tell the House that this legislation is not needed to stop bootlegging in British Columbia; bootlegging can be stopped by the bona fide prosecution of the bootlegger and lawbreaker and by discontinuing the present practice of playing politics with the liquor business. Just as soon as they stop that they can stop bootlegging, but you cannot mix up politics

Canada Temperance Act
and the selling of liquor and have good law or good liquor. Bootlegging, could be stopped by the government in this way, by importing and selling only good liquors at a fair price. What bootlegger could successfully compete with the government, buying on the wholesale scale that the government does and with the facilities it has for handling the goods? You might find an odd tramp walking about the streets with a flask in his hip pocket and selling a drink here and there for twenty-five cents, but that is a mere drop in the bucket. The Attorney General could stop the real bootlegging if he wanted to. [DOT]
As I said at the outset, the design of this legislation is not to stop bootlegging or to further moderation or temperance in the consumption of liquor. It is merely designed to give the Attorney General of British Columbia more power. The export warehouses are absolutely under the control of the government and can be checked up for every quart of liquor they handle. They can easily be put out of business by prosecution if they violate the law. It is alleged, I understand, by the Attorney General of British Columbia that these export and import warehouses are the cause of bootlegging. Well, he has them right under his hand at the present time and does not need this legislation to control them. The object of this legislation, I repeat, is to give the Control Board more power to force their spurious liquors upon the people of British Columbia. I must oppose this bill and I ask the government and the House not to force this legislation on the people of British Columbia without first consulting their wishes in the regular and constitutional way. Surely it is not too much to ask them whether they want it or not. The House has nothing to indicate that they want it except the word of the Attorney General who gives a reason that is not sound at all. If the bill had the sanction of the people of British Columbia or of the majority I would not question it for one moment; but it has not; it is unfair to them, and in my opinion should not go through.
I would like the House to observe that the effect of this bill when it is passed is to leave things just exactly as they are so far as the state of law and the administration of the law is concerned, but it does this; it gives the Attorney General of British Columbia the power to change it at his will. He need not necessarily change it, but he has the power there for control. If the bill came out-and-out in a manly way and said, this will be the law or that will be the law, the House might
very well pass judgment upon it, but why give the Attorney General of British Columbia this discretionary power to squeeze these people or not as he sees fit. I say that it is not- wise legislation, and I hope that the government will not force it through.

An exception is made for the government. Another exception was made for the exporters for their trade. They were allowed to import only	for their	trade	of exportation.
Since the second reading of the bill was adopted by this House I proposed myself that an addition should be made to the exception, to the effect that this should not apply to distillers in the province of British Columbia. Will the minister permit me to interrupt him. To make complete the objections he is reciting, we object and we claim that the Attorney General in conjunction with the proper officer of this government has that power now just as completely as this bill gives it to him. Secondly we claim that by this bill this parliament is foregoing its rights, transferring its rights into the hands of the Attorney General, without definitely stating that the importation will cease.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was going to sav to the hon. member that we do not intend to transfer that right to the Attorney General. The hon. member concluded his remarks yesterday by saying: "Well, I will not oppose the legislation" I understood that he was disposed to vote in its favour; but even with that declaration of his I want to try and satisfy all my hon. friends opposite and the people of British Columbia in this matter. I come here in all sincerity and I want to make the legislation I offer workable. There was a plebiscite in the province of British Columbia when the people, by a large majority, declared that they favoured a system of control by the government. This was supplemented by a resolution in the legislature of that province by which it is asked that we should now proceed to prohibit the importation of liquors and allow it only in favour of the government. The legislation which is before you, Mr. Chairman, is to that effect but I want to try to make its purpose as clear as possible. My hon. friends opposite object to the proviso that they found in the first, and second draughts. I am prepared to drop it. My hon. friends object also to licenses to exporters. Well, I am prepared to drop that. Now, my hon. friends cannot refuse to vote in support of the prohibition of importation except in favour of the government, because the people have already voted on the plebiscite and the legislature has requested this government to legislate in that direction. As all will remember, in the provinces where prohibition was adopted by the people and ratified by the executive, there is1 an exception in favour of manufacturers and brewers. speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And when it is applied there will be two exceptions, one in favour of the government and one in favour of the distillers. But the whole act goes into effect by the will of the Lieutenant Governor in Council. In that regard I would like to impress an argument on the minister and see whether it has any effect upon him or not. I approach it this way: Constitutionally there are certain important powers that are exclusively the possession of the provinces. There are other important powers exclusively the possession of the Dominion. It is admitted that the sovereign jurisdiction of the provinces in respect of theirs is on a level with the sovereign jurisdiction of the Dominion in respect of ours. It is also admitted that there can be no assignment from one to the other; from the Dominion to a province, or from the province to a Dominion, of any
powers. That either must act, not only in spirit but in letter, up to those requirements, those constitutional requirements. The Doherty Act provided another method, if I may so describe it, of giving what are Dominion powers to a province. It 4 p.m. gives the Dominion powers to a province in this way and subject to these precautions: The Doherty Act says that in every province which has a law living up to certain definite requirements of prohibition there shall be certain provisions of a federal act applied, the provisions being the prevention of importation with certain exceptions. The precautions are these: That first of all a majority of the legislature shall petition to have the federal act applied thereby bringing into effect within the province alone a federal law arising out of exclusively federal jurisdiction. That is the first precaution that the Doherty Act provides. Now, it provides a second pre-. caution of very great importance: That notwithstanding the fact that a majority of the legislature petitions-what the legislature petitions for, indeed, is the plebiscite indicating the will first of the legislature -[DOT] notwithstanding that, and in addition to that, the people of the province themselves shall vote and, by a majority, shall declare their will that such federal law arising out -of federal jurisdiction shall apply. Those precautions are very great safeguards. Undoubtedly it would never be sound and never be for the public good that the Dominion parliament should consent to bestow upon a province the right to call into effect federal law, except with such safeguards. The minister goes much further than, that in this bill, and it seems to me, though he may argtie that it is not of vital or sweeping consequences, that he establishes a precedent that may be dangerous. He seeks now to bring into effect in a province a federal measure with none of these precautions, none of those safeguards at all. This is a federal measure, and its provisions may be called into effect in a province by the mere fiat of a lieutenant governor in council. I ask hon. members to remember that this bill is general and applies everywhere. The minister speaks of British Columbia; but whenever another province comes into the position of British Columbia, the bill will apply in that province. The minister says that in British Columbia the legislature has voted a resolution asking for such a bill. Very good. Another legislature may not do so; but the lieutenant governor in council at that time may nevertheless call this bill into effect or call it out of effect. Therefore, while the minister can plead the resolution of
Canada Temperance Act

a legislature in this ease, he can plead it only as applicable to the individual instance, and it in no way justifies the generality of his bill.
Next, he has not the safeguard that the majority of the people in that province must want this legislation. The legislature need take no responsibility as it has to in the case of legislation within its powers. It is not necessary, as a safeguard to this legislation going into effect, that the people must want this measure. A mere lieutenant governor in council may call this bill in effect in any province which has given to it government control over the sale of liquor, a power to sell liquor in that province. Surely the minister is going a very grave length from the constitutional standpoint, and a length that, it seems to me, is going to get this parliament into difficulties later on. Even in the present case he cannot plead the plebiscite in British Columbia. But if he could plead it, that would not answer to the charge I make against his bill, because his bill is general and it will apply in the future just as well as now, when possibly British Columbia will not want at all what it voted for two or three years ago. It may not want now what it voted for two or three years ago; but it will have to take it, if the Lieutenant Governor in Council says so, and the legislature will have no power to veto it.
I started out a moment ago to say that even in this case, the minister cannot plead the plebiscite of British Columbia. British Columbia never by any vote voted for such legislation to be in effect, as the Lieutenant Governor in Council can put it into effect if this bill passes. What did the people of British Columbia vote for? Presumably knowing the jurisdiction of their legislature, the limits of that jurisdiction, they voted to endow that legislature with control of the sale of liquor, that is, with power to sell liquor through a government institution. When they voted for that, they knew that if the legislature followed the vote of the majority, nevertheless there would be the right to import for private use. They knew that, so presumably they voted that the power of the legislature and its exercise should be concurrent with the right of importation. The minister could not say nay to that contention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What about the
resolution of the legislature?

I am dealing with the
people now. The minister should have interrupted me when I was dealing with the resolution. I will come to the resolution later if the minister wants me to refer to it again.

He cannot plead the vote of the people. The people voted just the other way; they voted that the legislature might establish, and they willed that it should establish, a board for the sale of liquor within the province. They voted, knowing that such institution and the operation of that institution would be concurrent with the right of private importation for private use. The minister is putting it within the power of their government, without recourse to the people at all, to impose upon the people something which they did not vote for, and which presumably they voted against.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot accept
the "presumably," because the question was only whether they were in favour of prohibition or in favour of control by the government. There was no question of importation.

There was the question of importation, for this reason. They voted for control by the government, for the government having the right itself to sell liquor in sealed packages; that is to say, government control, government monopoly within the province over the sale of liquor in sealed packages. But they voted, presumably knowing-and that is why I used the word "presumably"-that while such legislation was going into effect, they would have the right, not to sell, but to import for private use. Consequently the people must be presumed to have voted against the prevention of importation for private use. The minister is putting it within the power of the government of that province to put precisely the opposite into effect, that precisely opposite law being a law that can derive force only from enactment by the parliament of Canada.
I have covered both phases of the argument. The minister sweeps aside the safeguards that all along have been provided, where what is exclusively federal power is put into the hands of a province, and he passes a general law which will enable the lieutenant governor of any province, under certain conditions, to put into effect in that province legislation which is federal legislation, irrespective wholly of the will of the people of that province. The minister says that he is justified because of the resolution. I answer him again that he can plead that for the present the Legislature of British Columbia warns this bill. I may be making too sweeping a statement in his favour, because I have not heard the whole of the debate; but so far as I have heard it, he can plead for the present that the legislature of British Columbia wants this bill. He cannot plead that the people do; he has not the slightest ground to argue that the people do. Every circumstance, every

Canada Temperance Act
fact we know argues that the people do not want it. He can, however, argue that the legislature at the present time wants this bill, or it did last December. But I tell the minister again that he is passing a law that will enable the provincial government, no matter what the people may want, to bring into effect a federal law wholly against the will of the legislature and of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have the power to change it.

But is it right, sound, or for the public good, that a federal law, a law that derives force wholly from enactment by this parliament, should be allowed to be put into effect by order in council in a province irrespective altogether of the will of the people or of the legislature, and to say in effect, for four years or until some other lieutenant governor, notwithstanding any vote of the people, may choose to wipe it away? I am presenting the case from the constitutional standpoint to the minister, and I venture to say, if the minister had taken it into his own hands and reviewed this phase of it, then, as a result of conditions that I have presented to him now, and that would have arisen to his mind he would have never made himself the party chiefly, responsible for legislation of this character.

In rising to say a few words on the question before the committee, I should like to assure the Minister of Justice that British Columbia is not entirely represented in the section of the House, to my right. We members here do not want to occupy the time of the House for hours talking politics, nor to influence the vote that will be taken in Manitoba this summer. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has been referring to British Columbia and telling the House what the people want out there. I want that hon. gentleman to understand that I represent over one-third of British Columbia, and was sent here by a majority of over 3,200 in excess of the man who ran to support the hon. leader of the Opposition, and I say that the people of the province of British Columbia do want the act that is proposed, and say it without hesitation. It has been repeatedly stated here that the whiskey in British Columbia is no good, and hon. gentlemen refer to it as "prune juice". Two hon. members yesterday afternoon said that they had not known the taste of whiskey for quite a long time. Well, I do know the taste of whiskey, and I am here to say that since the act passed in British Columbia I have got no bad whiskey from the Liquor Control Board of the province. I have never had a drink of poor whiskey from that source yet, and I have taken enough of it to know the difference between good and bad. I can assure the committee that the government in British Columbia is asking for the act; the government desires to get this control. A plebiscite was voted upon by the people of the province and was carried by a majority of nearly 35,000. The people of that province requested the present government to take control of (he liquor of British Columbia, and that same government is in power yet. 'The government feel that they cannot control the liquor situation properly under the present act and they come to this parliament and ask to be given further power. Is that unreasonable? I think that the government of British Columbia are entitled to it.
A great deal of insinuation has been cast at the Attorney General of the province of British Columbia, as well as other members of the local government. I think it should be beneath any member of this House to say a word or cast any insinuation against any member of another legislative body, nor do I think that it becomes any of us to speak disparagingly of those persons who represent the people of the province of British Columbia.
That is a good lesson.

Those gentlemen are not here to defend themselves, and hon. gentlemen in this chamber should bear in mind that if they are to carry the dignity of members of parliament it behooves them to let others alone. Let hon. gentlemen here look after their own affairs. Now, a great deal has been said about the influence that government control is having in British Columbia. One hon. gentleman yesterday wanted to read a whole front page of a newspaper in regard to the matter. I am not going to do that, but I desire to make a few statements in reference to the effect that prohibition has had and is having on some people; it may be interesting for us to know the facts. There is one district in the United States, not a very large district either, where in twelve months 9,401 illicit stills were seized. To carry the whiskey from these stills to the consumers there were in use 309 automobiles, 60 rigs and 93 horses, all of which were seized. These conveyances were carrying the product of these stills around the country. With what effect? In twelve days 103 persons lost their lives through this moonshine that came from these stills, and there were 37 cold-blooded murders in one city on the other side of the international line.

Because I

I can foresee a case, if it

I cannot let this clause pass without challenging at least a portion of it. Sections 40 and 41 set forth those who are not desirable as Canadian citizens and who can be deported on account of their misdemeanors, and bo on. Section 41 as set out in the bill distinctly provides that-
Any person. . . . who shall by word or act create or attempt to create riot or public disorder in Canadashall be classed as undesirable. The definition of "Canadian citizen" as set forth in the act is as follows:
"Canadian citizen" means-
I.	A person born in Canada who has not become an alien;
II.	A British subject who has Canadian domicile.
In order to get Canadian domicile he must be here five years.
Oh, no.

That is what the act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

It says, "having been landed therein within the meaning of this act." cial. There is a provision in the act dealing with cases where deportation may be had on the ground of moral turpitude, but here is a case where a man gets mixed up, intentionally or unintentionally, in a riot, and for that he can be deported without trial. I really think that is going too far.
I wish to ask the Minister of Justice whether a British citizen is required to be in Canada five years before he acquires Canadian citizenship 01 British citizenship within Canada?
No.

The only reason why we confine it to Canadian citizenship is that we cannot turn a Canadian citizen out of his own country; there is no place to which he can be deported. Then there was repentance.

No repentance at ah.
What does the hon. member want to put that word in for all the time? Because we passed legislation for a particular time, and stated it to be so, and the period passing we come and move the House to repeal it, we are only acting in accordance with the dictates of common sense. But the Senate voted it down. I feel safe in saying that a majority of those against it were of the Liberal party.
I think not.

I do, and I think I am correct. Of those for the legislation naturally a majority adhered to the government's view. Not all, I know many were opposed to it; but the majority, I think, of those opposed were of the Liberal party. Consequently, the legislation failed to pass. I speak now subject to correction but I think this government introduced legislation repealing it, or was it the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg, tMr. Woodsworth) ?
It did not get through the House.
Apparently under the government supported by my hon. friend.
The committee reported against it.

The committee reported against it? Very well, that is the situation. And the government appointed the committee. So, apparently, there was no very great sincerity in all the roar there was against the legislation. Let me put that before the mind of the hon. member for North'Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray). Apparently the essential part, the heart, of that legislation is still to remain I am making no particular complaint. Personally I would rather have it go; I do not think there is reason for it now. I am thoroughly convinced that there was necessity for it, thoroughly convinced that it rendered good service, that it helped to tide over a very serious situation, and that under it no specific injustice was done. I do not know whether there was one deported under it or not but it served as a deterrent. If there was any there was none save one whose deportation was recommended by an investigator, a member of the bench of Manitoba. But there was no abuse of the legislation whatever. The antagonism to it was purely political, antagonism for votes. That is now demonstrated by the subsequent repeal of the section.
My right hon. friend is in error.
In what?
That this section applied only to one man. Under my right hon. friend's government it was applied solely to British subjects.
Yes?
To Englishmen, Irishmen and Scotchmen.
Then I was right in my statement.
My right hon. friend approved, and still approves, of the passing of an act that would deport British subjects from this country without trial by a jury.
Why not deport British subjects, if undesirable, from this country just as much as aliens? I would be in favour of deporting any person who was undesirable.

What I stated was that I did not think there was any deportation under it but that if there was a deportation there was only one recommended by an investigator; a member of the bench of Manitoba. The hon. member says there was none at all deported.

Not then.

Immigration Act
That is exactly what I said.

I think the real ground for not doing it was the protest made by the people of Winnipeg. What absolutely prohibited it from being done was the feeling aroused in that city. I ask my right lion, friend if there were not strong representations from all over Canada to change that policy.
And very strong recommendations not to make any change.

I can hardly understand what the minister means when he says there were no representations made to him with regard to the further amendment of this act. Last year I introduced a bill which was pretty thoroughly discussed in committee and came before this House looking not merely at the emendation of section 41 but to the radical reconstruction of the act. The recommendation of the committee was that the . entire act should be redrafted at the coming session. That recommendation to the House last year is not in any sense carried out by the present amendments, but simply a slight modification of one or two clauses. Again this year I had the privilege of spending some time with the acting minister over some of these clauses, and urged as strongly as I could-and I had a considerable body of opinion be-
5 p.m. hind me-that there should be changes not merely in respect of one or two clauses but of the whole principle of the bill.
It does seem to me that we are here faced very clearly with a large issue, the issue, as to whether citizens or residents of this country shall have the right to a fair trial. I was very much interested to hear the leader of the Opposition say that the time had gone by when this kind of legislation is necessary. We would differ as to whether it was ever necessary, as I take it that the time when we most need the safeguards of the law is when there is some extraordinary excitement. There was a time of hysteria several years ago and it was during that time we needed the law to safeguard men from those who were caught up by the hysteria. It was at that time this law was passed-a law which took away all safeguards and deprived men who had been in this country for years, whether of British or of foreign birth, of the right to a trial by jury. I think it was little less than a plot which was organized at that time that placed on the statute book legislation by which men were to be deported from Canada without trial by jury. However, that is past and if there is a reflection on the Conservative government-the government in power in 1919-for having passed legislation of that kind at that time I would say that the leader of the Opposition is right when he says that the reflection is even greater on the present government when two or three years after that trouble, they refuse to repeal an obnoxious act of this nature. It ought to be known to every British subject of this country born outside Canada that today he has absolutely no right to trial by jury. That has not seemed to enter the consciousness of a good many men who were born outside of Canada. I say "British born" because, speaking frankly, that is a good basis on which to appeal. I do not want to stress that unduly. I think the hon. member across the way is right when he says that everyone -whether British born or alien born-ought to have the protection of the laws in this country. But it does seem to me that the British born should be stirred up a little bit when they reflect that when they crossed the ocean to this country they forfeited this right which we have all been told has belonged to Britishers ever since the time of the Magna Charta and the Bill of Rights.
Now coming to particular clauses I would say that the key to the whole situation lies in the definitions. According to sub-section (i) of section 2-this is chapter 25 "An Act to amend the Immigration Act":
(i) Canadian domicile can only be acquired, for the -purposes of this act, by a person having his domicile for at least five years in Canada after having been landed therein within the meaining of this act.
That would seem to show that any immigrant to this country, whether an alien or a British born person, may acquire Canadian domicile in five years and that having acquired Canadian domicile he is protected. But that is not so because a little further down we find this clause:
-and provided further that no person who belongs to the prohibited or undesirable classes within the meaning of section forty-one of this act shall be capable of acquiring Canadian domicile.
There is where the difficulty lies. It is all very well to say that a man who has been five years in this country acquired Canadian domicile; but if for reasons thereinafter enumerated he is considered to be undesirable within the meaning of the act he becomes incapable of acquiring Canadian domicile whether he has been here five years or twenty years. The safeguards which he ought to have are taken away.
Now if we turn to the other sections, we find that there are a variety of reasons under which people may be considered as being
Immigration Act

undesirable. It is quite true that slight modifications are being proposed in section 41; but the other sections are not being modified, and they will still leave anybody bom outside of this country liable to deportation. For instance, there are these three clauses:
(n)	Persons who believe in or advocate the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Canada or of constituted law and authority, or who disbelieve in or are opposed to organized government, or who advocate the assassination of public officials, or who advocate or teach the unlawful destruction of property.
I do not think any one in th,is House is going to advocate the things which this section' seeks to prohibit. But that is not the point. The point is that a man may be accused of doing these things, and if he is accused of doing these things, he may be deported without opportunity of being heard by a court. What we are arguing for is that he should have a fair trial and be judged as to whether he is guilty of these things or not. I know the attitude of some of us has been absolutely misrepresented in this regard, and that because we were trying to safeguard the individual, it has been said that we are advocating all these things that are being prohibited in this legislation. That is not the case. We are advocating the safeguarding of every man, by insisting that he shall be given the right of trial by jury. The next paragraph reads:	,
(o)	Persons who are members of or affiliated with any organization entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government, or* advocating or teaching the duty, necessity or propriety of the unlawful assaulting or killing of any officer or >fficers, either of specific individuals or of officers senerally, of the government of Canada or of any other >rganized government, because of his or their official character, or advocating or teaching the unlawful lestruction of property;
Here again, these things that are mentioned are doubtless unsocial in their character; but the question is one of interpretation. For example, the first clause reads:
Persons who are members of or affilated with any organization entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government.
That may easily be interpreted as applying to anyone who criticizes the government. As regards the last clause:
Or advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property.
Supposing a strike occurred, as, for instance, was the case last year in the Cape Breton district, and the men who were in charge of the property or working on the property quit work. It might be said that there was danger of flooding of the mines, and that possibly destruction of property might be caused thereby.

This clause might be interpreted to mean that any man who advocated that the men should quit work under such circumstances, and possibly bring about a loss of property, would thereby under this clause be regarded as undesirable and liable to deportation without trial. I am not advocating the destruction of property; I am not here defending the man who seeks to destroy property. That is not the point. I urge that a man accused of such things ought to be tried before his peers, given a fair chance to present his case, and not shuffled out of the country without a trial. There is a similar objection to paragraph (p), the next following:
(p)	Enemy aliens or persons who have been alien enemies and who were or may be interned on or after the 11th day of November, 1918, in any part of His Majesty's dominions or by any of His Majesty's allies.
I think that is one of the clauses that, it is suggested, should be changed, and I am very glad that change is being made, because here again certain men, many thousands of them in western Canada who are technically alien enemies feel very bitterly the injustice of being brought under this act. An Austrian friend of mine said to me during the war: "Austria was an enemy of ours"

he was a Galician, a Ukrainian-"long before she was an enemy of Great Britain's. We came to this country in order to get away from Austrian control." This man was technically an alien enemy and, coming under this clause, he was liable to deportation as an undesirable. It became absolutely impossible for him ever to acquire Canadian citizenship, though he might have been five years or twenty-five years in Canada. This question of domicile is to me the most serious part of the act, and one that is not being touched by the amendments which the minister has introduced. It seems to me that we ought to have such a thorough-going revision of this act that it would not be possible for any man who has been resident five years in Canada to be deported without trial. I think that is clear, and a great responsibility is put on the Liberal government of this country if they will allow it to be said, when there is no trouble in Canada at all, that they refuse to repeal legislation under which it is quite possible to deport British-born subjects without trial.

I have
noticed a number of telegrams in the hands of hon. members, and I have one myself from the Shipping Federation of Montreal protesting against section 8 which provides for fines to be imposed. But inasmuch as the bill is to remain in committee I am prepared to hear representations which, if they are reasonable, I shall be glad to consider. I would point out, however, that we experience considerable difficulty in connection with this very matter. Ship-masters come into a port and are careless about the care of their crew some of whom perhaps desert, and we have great trouble apprehending them at times. The worst feature of this is that very frequently a man who gets into the country in this way is a person who would not be able to pass the immigration officer. We know of a case in point at the moment. A seaman deserted and afterwards became ill; he is now a public charge of Canada and has
been for the past year. I am convinced therefore that we need this section, and I do not think it will create any hardship on shipowners. It will, of course, create a hardship if they allow seamen to desert without duly presenting them to the immigration officer for inspection before entering.

I have received the following telegram from the secretary of the Shipping Federation; he says:
Seventy-two thousand seamen passed through this port last season and accounted for under the shipping acts controlled by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Immigration Act gradually usurping control from proper officers under shipping acts causing duplication of work. Each seaman is provided with continuous discharge book with his record as to conduct and ability which is checked up by proper officers at this port at beginning and end of voyage Seamen are regarded as specially privileged class and any interference with them liable cause retaliation by other nations. Respectfully ask before any action taken that the Shipping Federation of Canada be given opportunity being heard before committee of House.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is absolutely no attempt on the part of the department to interfere with the Shipping Federation, but we do desire to protect ourselves and I think we are right in doing so. Why should the people of Canada through the negligence of a shipmaster b'e called upon to pay for the care of a mariner who deserts and becomes a public charge? We are simply taking steps to protect ourselves, and if that is an injury to shipping, then I am afraid we shall have to insist on its being done.
I understand that the bill is to remain in committee until a delegation waits upon the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The position of the master of a vessel is a very difficult one. It is rather hard to tell whether any particular member of a crew intends to desert,. During the very short experience I had with the Customs department I know that there were cases that came before the department that were quite painful, where vessels were liable for a fine because of the improper acts of some members of the crew-acts that could scarcely be detected even, by the greatest vigilance on the part of the officers. When you find seamen practically conspiring to leave a vessel, it seems to me you are putting a very heavy burden upon the master or the shipowner if you impose penalties for the acts of members of the crew. Generally they are in a state of antagonism, and certainly the master is not at all likely'' to be in the confidence of the seamen. That is one point
Immigration Act

I would stress. I know that, the minister wants his law to be fair above all things. While I do not ordinarily take the position,, yet I feel that the stress of the war period having passed, it might not be out of place to consider with regard to deportation whether, if not a jury, which is not always the best way of determining questions, at least some form of tribunal of the department, if not a judicial body, could not be instituted to hear both sides of the case before a man is deported. It is usually very easy for an official getting information from one side only to form a prejudice against a particular individual. I admit that he is not likely to be prejudiced; I admit that in all probability, if there is a complaint, the person complained against will be found to deserve deportation. But still there is always the chance that a false story may be given credence and a man may be unjustly used. I think we all agree, irrespective of any shade of party in the House, that the best recommendation for our Canadian institutions is the ability and the willingness to do clear and full justice in every instance. I should like to see an opportunity given every man to be heard in his own, behalf before sentence of deportation is pronounced against him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That opportunity is always given even in cases where we reject people who endeavour to enter the country. There is no hasty taking hold of an individual and bundling him out of the country. I agree with much that my hon. friend has said. So far I have not had to deal with a single case of the kind, so that I have no personal experience in regard to seamen. But I am dealing daily with cases of entry into Canada, where the individual has no claim on earth upon the country but is simply seeking to get into Canada. In every such case we give the fullest opportunity for him to present his case. Not only that; he is kept for a period in which he may substantiate any claims he makes in order that he may establish his fitness to enter the country. It is not likely therefore that we shall be harsh on any person who has any sort of claim upon us. My hon. friends from British Columbia, I might say here will protest most strenuously against any latitude in this matter. They will say that this is one of the methods employed by shipping people to get orientals
[Mr. Baxter.!
into the country without the knowledge of the Department of Immigration. It is obvious that we must be fairly drastic with shipping coming into the ports of the country. What is the incentive for the mariner to avoid the immigration officer? He would be admitted into the country the same as any other individual if he passed through the proper channel, and it is quite evident therefore, in nine cases out of ten, that he avoids the immigration officer simply because he anticipates trouble in being passed. So that the only recourse we have is to be fairly drastic with the shipmaster.

The minister will find, I think, that he has power enough under what we might call the Chinese exclusion act-because that is practically what it is-to deal with Chinese; and by similar means he will be able to cope with Japanese. But the general Immigration Act must deal with people who are not within the prescribed Asiatic classes. I am not finding the least fault with anything the department deems it best to do; I have no criticism to offer because I have no particular knowledge of the subject. One likes, however, to see the law always provide an opportunity for the under dog to be heard, and I think that is only fair. The minister, I am sure, agrees with the sentiment; the only question is as to how far we go respectively in practice.

I would make a suggestion
to the minister when he is reconsidering section 3. There seems to be some doubt and difference of opinion as to when a British subject becomes a Canadian citizen. It is fully understood that the alien has the advantage in knowing the specific time when he becomes a Canadian citizen by reason of his being naturalized. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray) says it requires five years' domicile for a British subject to become a Canadian citizen; other members on the government side do not agree with him. It seems to me that a clause might well be inserted whereby a British subject living in this country would know definitely when he becomes a Canadian citizen.
