House again in committee on Bill No. 85 to amend the Naturalization Acts, 1914 and 1920, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 4-Repeals:

How does this
matter now stand? I rather understood that the minister was making inquiries regarding certain suggestions as to consolidation of the law.	.

Consideration of this bill stood
over last week on the application of my hon. friend for St. John (Mr. Baxter) that a memorandum be made with regard to consolidating these acts. Such a memorandum was prepared and forwarded to him.

I do not know whether it will be effectual or not, but the substance of this memorandum in itself constitutes, I think, the very strongest argument in favour of the position which I took that it would be well to consolidate the law. I have gone over the pamphlet with great care and find there are what I might call detached portions of legislation that really have no relation to anything and I think can do no possible good. Then again I find in this pamphlet, which I might call the Red Book, a most absolute misinterpretation of the law. It is really astonishing to me that reputable officers of the Civil Service should send out a document so misleading. I have gone very carefully into the question debated by my right hon. leader and I am satisfied that the statement in the red pamphlet that the Secretary of State can grant naturalization even against an adverse report is absolutely untenable from a legal standpoint. Those who have contended that it was necessary first that there should be a favourable report, and that then the minister might refuse, are absolutely right. No lawyer could possibly give a different opinion.
Now, I should like to call the minister's attention to this white pamphlet. If he compared it with the Dominion act he would find that the words at about line 23, "Provided that the child of a British subject" should go up after line 4. The whole thing here as reprinted is a jumble and does not reflect any credit whatever on those who compiled it. I have gone through the pamphlet section by section and must say that the whole is a very fair almost a literal, reproduction of the Imperial legislation. Some slight alterations are made, as for instance in section 7, where in England they have a committee instead of a commission to investigate the standing of an alien, and the Secretary of State acts directly, while here it is done by the Governor in Council. I cannot see any objection to this; it is pretty much a matter of formality.
The really substantial objection to the bill, however, is in the repeal of pactically sections 19 to 24 and allowing section 25 to stand as the vital part. This committee,
I think, will have to pass upon the question of whether naturalization should be the sole prerogative of the Secretary of State working through any agencies which he may prescribe by regulations, which will be unknown to the people to be affected and to the rest of the public until those regulations are promulgated; or whether we shall have some system, not necessarily a county court judge, but some tribunal which will be local in its character causing as little expense and labour to the person seeking to be naturalized as well may be, and yet providing some efficient inquiry into his standing and character. The bill would be better if the Secretary of State would insert in it that a prerequisite for naturalization should be a favourable report by the secret police of Canada-if such a body exists, and I think there is something answering to that description-or by the mounted police, or if he would prescribe something other than the jiere unrestrained will of an officer of the government. As the office is occupied at present I would not be doing any honour to my own province and I would not be doing justice to the personal friendship which has always existed between the hon. Secretary of State and myself if I made any reflections upon what he might do in his official capacity. I am quite willing to trust him individually, but if I contracted to trust him as Secretary of State I do not know to what that might commit me in the line of succession.

You might come into power.
Naturalization Acts

And then things might be a thousand times worse than my hon. friend imagines, because I fancy he has spent the greater part of his life in painting pictures of what one might call imaginary Toryism. As the witches in Macbeth put into their caldron everything nauseous and noxious, so he in his picture has imagined eveiything evil and labelled it "Toryism". But he has painted it conversely from a reflection in his memory of the virtues as he considers them, of the party with which he is associated.
The picture I was not painting, and one it would be useless to try to paint, was my hon. friend's imagination.

Do not attempt to gild refined gold, or paint the lily, or commit any of these other excesses. But really, apart from all politics-because this question of the right of citizenship is deserving of a higher type of discussion than the ordinary hustings style -do we not need some tribunal that will be known to the people, that will be readily accessible, and that will pass upon a man's qualifications for citizenship? I do not think that the county courts were bad so far as their dealings with this matter were concerned. I agree that the reports very often were not worth much, but that was due not to any want of care on the part of the judges but to the fact that they had no officer and no money that they could employ for the making of investigations. They have had to deal simply with affidavits or with the persons who were presented to them or came before them. They had to make the best investigation they could under the circumstances, and naturally it fell far short of completeness. I know cases where county court judges have been assiduous in shutting out the class of people whom they looked upon as undesirable, and I give them credit for doing the best they could. The mounted police, however, do not extend to all parts of Canada, and I do not know how you could get a report in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island-that is the part of the universe I know most about. You might get it from a member of parliament, but perhaps he would not know anything more about a man than whether or not he was likely to be a friendly voter, and that is not what we want. The mounted police do not go down there unless they are sent for in a case of emergency. There is a branch of the Dominion police-I do not know what you call it-which assists the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue in the enforcement of the narcotic drug law and that sort of thing, and it is possible that an investiga-

tion under this act might be made by that branch. But that would be a matter of regulation under this act. Why not make it possible to read the statute through and be informed by it what particular officer would investigate a man's character? I should be willing if the minister would provide that what I would call unofficially the secret police of Canada should make a report upon each case and subipit it to the county court judge. There you have effective machinery; you are sure of an investigation. These police know pretty well the malefactors throughout the Dominion, and their work would not be partisan or political. I admit frankly that the section that the Secretary of State desires to preserve is practically an exact reproduction of the British section, and it may be said that if it is good enough for Great Britain it should be good enough here. Well, there is all the difference in the world between the settled, steady and orderly administration of the British official departments and the political interference which has so often occurred in this country.
Does my hon. friend Suggest that there are no politics in Great Britain?
Great Britain is rampant with politics, but there is not very much immigration into Great Britain.
Not much immigration?

If there is much immigration into Great Britain, the failure of this regulative system is demonstrated by the millions of pounds that Great Britain had to pay in order to extirpate in time of war the German spies who had got in in time of peace under this very set of regulations, without proper inquiry into their characters. And that is the system that my hon. friend, by inference, supports and wants to have introduced into this country.
Does my hon. friend not think that these Germans could have got into England notwithstanding any such system?

If Great Britain had realized how dangerous these people were and had determined to exclude them, I am confident they would not have got in. My hon. friend will agree that immigration laws can be enforced.

Now that Great Britain is legislating in the light of her experience in the late war, why is it that no change has been made with respect to the naturalization of Germans and their entry into the country?

Naturalization Acts

My hon. friend will have to ask the statesmen of Great Britain for an answer to that question. If I may again, at my own peril, exercise my imagination, I presume the reason is that Great Britain is to-day, as she always has been in the past, too magnanimous to traitors. I only repeat that in point of form it would be much better to bring down a consolidated measure, even if that necessitated a delay until next year.
I would like the Secretary of State to consider the re-establishment or the continuance of some form of local tribunal such as we are accustomed to, aiding it in any way he likes by reports from any investigators, police or others who can give that assistance. But let us have the investigation in the community where the proposed British subject lives and moves and has his being, where a fair inquiry can be made. Do not let us test the fitness of a man simply by long range correspondence with Ottawa.

This bill as introduced is a rather innocent looking bill, but it deals wth one of the most important matters that can possibly come before this parliament, namely, our citizenship. The two questions involved are, first, as to the procedure in connection with naturalization, and, secondly,-this is the more important one, it seems to me-whether we are to cheapen or depreciate the value of British citizenship. Some confusion existed in the minds of many hon. members when this bill was introduced because of the contention then made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) to the effect that under section 2 there rested in him an absolute discretion as to the granting of a certificate of naturalization and that this provision was entirely apart from and independent of the provisions contained in sections 19 to 24 inclusive. I submit that a careful reading of the statute would convince the minister that the application referred to in section 2 is really the application that is referred to in sections 19 to 24. Whatever doubt there may be as to the law as it has heretofore existed, there can be no doubt as to the effect of this amendment, which is to place entirely in the discretion of the minister the granting in any and every case of a certificate of naturalization.
If this amendment is accepted by the House then there will be no provision in the statute for investigation. There will be nu publicity in connection with the application. There will be no lapse of time necessary, as now exists, between the filing of the application and the granting of the certificate. The minister pointed out that in some cases the notice
of the application might be posted inconspicuously or might not be seen. I submit that if the notice of application is posted in the office of the Clerk of the Peace and remains there for three months, and the application is then brought to the court and is there dealt with with all the regularity, with all the solemnity and with all the publicity that undoubtedly attends these applications, being read at the opening of the court in the presence of the jurors, the witnesses and the whole attendance at the court, there is a large measure of publicity involved in that. What does the minister propose to substitute for that publicity? Absolutely nothing is provided in this bill. What safeguards are provided? None do [DOT]we find in this bill.
Why are these changes proposed? Who is asking for them? And what is the reason that they are brought forward at this time? It seems to me that the possibilities of the manipulation of naturalization certificates are very dangerous indeed if this bill goes through. If it is passed, what will be its effect and what will be the procedure? We can easily imagine some ambitious political candidate ascertaining the names of all those who are available for naturalization in his constituency, getting a set of forms filled out and coming down to the minister and urging speed and haste in determining these applications, and then going back with a bunch of naturalization certificates and passing them out to these people. I do not suggest that the minister has anything of that kind in mind, but I submit that it is all possible under the provisions of this bill. I do not think the minister ought to allow himself to be led into any such temptation as that.
I am safe.
He may be able to resist it but "Let him that tliinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall."
I would not be tempted even if my hon. friend came and asked me to do this thing for him.

I would not expect to be troubled with it because there are not many aliens in the part of the province from which I come. The minister's successor may not be-as capable of resistance to temptation as the minister imagines himself to be in this particular respect. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is possible that these certificates might be peddled for political party purposes, and I do not think the House should pass any legislation that would make that possible. We should safeguard our citizenship, which we appreciate very highly. Our

Naturalization Acts
neighbours to the south have had a rather sorrowful experience I think in connection with matters of this kind. Their citizenship has been depreciated and treated as of little value. We do not desire that in Canada. The alien who comes to reside with us should be impressed with the importance and value of British citizenship, and the responsibility which it imposes. The procedure provided by this bill is not calculated to bring that result. '
The minister in the course of his address when the bill was introduced made some reflections upon the way in which the judges conduct these investigations. Speaking from my own knowledge in the province of Ontario I do not think there is any ground for any such complaint. These applications are dealt with in the same manner as any other item of court business, and the judges give the matter the careful and proper attention which it deserves.
I am opposed therefore to this bill in its present form because it is calculated, I think, to increase the expense in connection with the naturalization of aliens. It leaves the matter entirely at the discretion of the Secretary of State or other minister to whom the matter may be referred, and really creates him an autocrat in this matter. It leads to centralization. It removes the safeguards that at present exist in connection with the granting of these certificates, and does not provide for any reasonable or proper investigation before certificates are granted. It is capable of manipulation for political party purposes, and worse than all the most serious objection to the bill is that it tends to cheapen and depreciate the value of British citizenship.

At the last sitting the minister argued that he had power no matter what may have been the report of the judge, under section 23, to grant naturalization, that his power in this respect was absolute, that he did not need any favourable report. I contended at the time, he will remember, that he did under the law as it stands to-day require first a favourable report from the judge before he could exercise his discretion at all, and I suggested that he procure the opinion of the Justice department on the point. May I ask the minister if he has procured it.

I may say to my hon. friend
that I did not understand him to ask me to get an opinion from the Justice department.

I suggested it and expressed considerable confidence as to what it would be.
(Mr. H. A Stewart.]

It has not been referred to the Justice department particularly, but it has been looked into very carefully by the legal officers of my department, and they are very strongly of the opinion that the statement I made is correct and that the administration as carried out is correctly in line with the act.

I really cannot hedp but say that the contention in my judgment is absurd. It is so manifest it is absurd, and I suggested at the last sitting that the opinion of the Justice department be procured. There must be some other clause or some other section that has not been drawn to my attention, that the minister has not referred to at all, if that can be the law. I do not think the minister should ask to go on with this legislation till he has produced the opinion of the Justice department on this point. Why, it is the whole point before the House. The minister would surely hardly dare to come to this House and ask that it confer on himself the whole jurisdiction in naturalization without any restraint whatever. Surely he would not. He says that has been the case before. I dispute it. It has not been the case before. Now then if he says I am wrong in that, I would like him to get the opinion of the Justice department of this government. Surely I am not asking for anything unreasonable. Even if the Justice department so rules, while it would be very strong in his support, I take the other view. But he should not come to this House unarmed with the opinion of that department and say to the House that the law as it stood before gave him unrestrained jurisdiction, that he is not asking now for any more unless he has the opinion of the Justice department at least to back him up.
I think this bill is audacious. It is an arrogant request to be brought forward particularly by those who have been ranting against autocracy and order in council government to seek to place in the hands of one of their own number the sole, unqualified control of the citizenship of Canada from this day on, naturalize whom they like and not naturalize whom they do not like, inquire where they like and not inquire where they do not like, ask whom they like and refuse to ask whom they do' not like, get information if they want to or do without it if they so prefer-all that put into the power of the minister in connection with naturalization in a country like Canada.
Canada is a country into which, in the past, we have had large waves of immigration. Our citizenship to-day is a citizenship that has come from immigration, in very large measure from the naturalization of aliens, and to place

Naturalization Acts
that vast power in the hands of a minister
without any restraint or without any necessary preparation at all, is, I say, an audacious and arrogant request and I do not think it should be done. It never was intended before, I do not think it ever was the law before; in fact I feel entirely convinced it was not. I must say that I have observed with pleasure very considerable hesitancy on the part of lawyers sitting around my hon. friend against staking their professional reputations on asserting that under the law as it stood the minister could naturalize without first having received the favourable report of the investigating judge; there seems to be no possible reading of the legislation that will bring that result. So if the minister argues for this at all he should not do so on the authority of the law officers. I do not know who the law officer of his department is, but the law officer upon whom ministers should rely is the Department of Justice. Let the minister bring an opinion from the Department of Justice at least before he asks to go on with this legislation.

When my right hon. friend asks for information respecting any legislation emanating from the government it is only fair that it should be given to him; but when he suggests that in proposing the present bill I am acting arrogantly I do not think he is treating me with fairness. When this bill was up before I stated that the matter was one which had given the department a great deal of concern, and that I was bringing the measure forward for the sole purpose of improving the Naturalization Act which was placed upon the statute book by my right hon. friend. If the proposed legislation is not right I am perfectly willing that any defect should be remedied. If it is wrong to leave discretion in this matter entirely in the hands of the Secretary of State I, for one, am quite prepared to have that wrong righted. But I do say this to my right hon. friend: During the time I have had the administration of this act, I have found that the inquiry provided for under the statute, from the reports of the county court judges that have come to me, has been of no avail or value. Now I am quite willing to accept the suggestion-

Does the minister make that as a general assertion? He may have cases where the reports do not appear to be of value, but surely he does not ask us to believe that the statement is true generally? I have seen the judges in action-
So have I.

Very well. The fact that what my hon. friend says is true in certain cases would not justify the sweeping assertion he has made. I have not seen any cases except those where the duties were carefully discharged.

If my right hon. friend will refer to the debates which took place during the passage of the acts of 1914 and of 1919, as well as the act of 1920, he will find that the Minister of Justice of that day and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) took exactly the opposite view and that the investigation, in regard to naturalization, was regarded as a huge joke.

I should like to say a few words on this question of Canadian citizenship. To my mind this is one of the most important things we have discussed in this House, and it is time now we were beginning to correct some of the mistakes we made in the past. The mistake we made in the past seems to be that we regarded Canadian citizenship too lightly. Canadian citizenship, and the privileges that go with it, is something that is not to be lightly given or lightly taken away once it has been given. These are two mistakes that were made in the past. Canadian citizenship ought to be a privilege valued very highly by the Canadians, just as Roman citizenship was highly valued. I remember reading of one who said: "With a great price I obtained this freedom." But the man to whom he was speaking was able to retort: "But I was free born." We who are free bom are very proud of the fact; but we ought to urge upon those who acquire Canadian citizenship by a price, that they should also be proud of it. Therefore, it is something that ought not to be too easy of attainment. While I would not like to put any unnecessary obstacles in the way of those who have fulfilled the conditions of Canadian citizenship, neither would I like to make it so easy of attainment that they would consider it as of but little value. Unfortunately, in the past the method by which large bunches
Naturalization Acts

of foreigners have been given Canadian citizenship has not reflected credit upon us, nor has this been done in such a manner as to make those people esteem the privilege very highly.
I would sincerely regret if the bestowal of or the refusal to bestow Canadian citizenship should rest entirely in the hands of one man, no matter how good a man he might be. It would be presumptuous for a layman to undertake to express an opinion as to the interpretation of the law as it stands, although 1 have an opinion of what that interpretation should be, and I certainly have a clear idea as to what I think the law ought to be. I do not know whether the courts have functioned satisfactorily in the past. That is a matter with which I have had very little, indeed practically nothing to do; but if the. courts have not functioned satisfactorily in the past, would it not be better to try to secure such amendments and arrangements as would assure that they do function satisfactorily, and thus make it perfectly certain that the proper inquiry should be made, that the proper steps should be taken, not necessarily with the absolute holding up of the proceedings, but so to delay them as to ensure that everything was done, calmly, deliberately and judiciously? Thus when the time comes for one of these foreigners who have come amongst us, to make his home here and to be naturalized, it should be impressed upon him that it is no small privilege that is being bestowed upon him; that it is something he might look forward to. In this we have again failed in our duty. We might have made it a great part of our educational system to instil into the minds of the children of these people, that it was a day to be looked forward to when their parents and they, through their parents, might enter into the privileges of Canadian citizenship. We sometimes think our friends across the line have gone too far in the matter of flag-waving; but they have laid a great deal of emphasis upon the privilege of American citizenship, whereas we have failed in some degree in the past in not laying sufficient emphasis upon Canadian citizenship and the privileges that go with it. I would wish that this parliament at this time would take such steps in such deliberate manner as would ensure that the next act that appears lpon our statute books shall be such as to fulfil all the conditions of fairness and justice to those that come amongst us to make their homes in Canada, and at the same time such as to ensure that those whom we take into our family, shall be fully impressed with our ideals and institutions, and with the desire 
to help us to make Canada what we would like it to be.

I presume this is the proper place for me to move an amendment which would take the place of section 4. I would move to insert after section 3 a new section to be known as section 4, reading as follows:
Subsection (e) of subsection (2) of section 7 of the Naturalization Acts, 1914 and 1920, is hereby amended by striking out the first two lines and substituting therefor the following:
(e) Remains, according to the law of any foreign state, a subject of that state.
The original clause reads as follows. This is amongst the list of people whom the minister can de-naturalize, if I may use such a word. I am putting in the words "those who":
Those who remain, according to the law of a state at war with His Majesty, a subject of that state.
In other words, I am applying to peace time conditions that were formerly inserted in case of war. The object of my amendment is to prevent a man from being a citizen of more than one country at the same time. While my remarks apply more particularly to those of the Japanese race in British Columbia, I wish to emphasize the point that I do not want to draw the debate along the lines of the necessity, or advisability, or lack of advisability of oriental immigration, because that has nothing whatever to do with the matter. Neither do I wish to make a plea for or against naturalization of orientals. I may have views on that subject but that is not the point at issue. I wish to confine this debate on the amendment purely to this point: Is it desirable that a man shall be a citizen of two countries at the same time? I might also say that it is about as feasible and reasonable to expect a man to be loyal to two countries at the same time, as it is to suggest that a woman should be faithful to two men at the same time. The propositions are somewhat allied.
We know when a man is naturalized, especially if he is of mature age before being naturalized, he will always retain a certain sympathy for the country of his origin. We expect that even under most favourable conditions. All we ask of him is that he dissociate himself from his country of origin, and show a genuine desire to affiliate himself with the country of his adoption. I propose to show that in the case of this particular race, the Japanese, the Japanese government maintains the closest jurisdiction, -for that is the proper word-control and,
I think I can say, practically government over its nationals in a case like this. They

Naturalization Acts
do not pretend to expatriate them or allow them to be expatriated. I maintain therefore that under these conditions this supposed naturalization of Japanese as British subjects is more or less, and a good deal more than less, a farce.
It is a well-known fact throughout the civilized world that the British Crown stands behind British subjects, and no trouble or expense is too great to right the wrongs of those subjects or to vindicate their wrongful death. But once a citizen of the British Empire has forfeited his rights under the British Crown, once he has alienated himself by adopting th,e nationality of another country, the British government has nothing more to do with him; it takes no more interest in him, but regards him entirely as an alien; which is an absolutely proper course to pursue. I am subject to correction, of course, but I do not believe there is another country in the world which to-day allows a man to be a citizen of two countries at the same time. It may be said that the United States does that, but the case is not parallel. The United States does not naturalize orientals at all, therefore the question cannot arise in that regard. In the United States they have a problem which is somewhat allied inasmuch as there are in that country a large number of Japanese bom in America who claim the right to vote there, and are still Japanese subjects; and there is a strong agitation going on now to deal with the matter. But the case is not exactly parallel to this.
Now, I am going to be very brief and I shall not go into any long quotations from pamphlets or other documents I want to quote however three sentences of the evidence given before the Fisheries Commission in British Columbia last year. There appeared before the commission a naturalized Japanese named Hoyuma Yonemura, who had been naturalized ten years, and these questions were asked him:
Q. Have you ever become expatriated from Japan? -A. No. '	-
Q. And you never made application for expatriation?-A. I did, but could not succeed. That expatriation is in question now in the House of Commons in Japan.
Q. Are all naturalized Japanese in this country still citizens of Japan according to the law of Japan?- A. Yes.
That is the sworn evidence of a Japanese naturalized British subject. Let me now quote from a book called "Facts," the pamphlet alluded to by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) who described it as propaganda. It is got out by the Japanese Consul General in Canada and I
shall not express any opinion as to the merits of it or its good taste, or as to whether or not it is propaganda. I want to quote it, being assured that what I quote is at least as favourable to Japan as it possibly can be made. I cannot be charged with exaggeration in order to prove my case when I quote from this source. I am quoting now from page 34:
The Japanese law concerning nationality. Article 20. In the case of a Japanese subject who has acquired foreign nationality by reason of birth in a foreign country and domicile in that country, he or she may be expatriated with the permission of the Minister of State for Home Affairs.
That is, they can be expatriated from Japan with the consent of the Japanese government. That seems reasonable; all they have to do is to ask permission. Well, there are two objections to that, and the first is that they do not do it. It is never, or hardly ever, done, and that is a fairly good reason for objecting to it. In the United States, which has always been a good example to take in this matter, because they are further along the line in the Japanese question than we are, there are some 90,000 American-born Japanese in Hawaii and continental America entitled to all the rights of American citizenship, and according to a statement made by the Foreign Office-that is to say, the United States Foreign Office, at Tokyo, in September, 1920, there had been only 73 applications from these 90,000 American-born Japanese for expatriation, and permission had been granted by the Japanese government in 64 cases. So that out of 90,000 men claiming to be citizens of the United States with the right to vote there at that time, two and a half years ago, only 73 applications had been made for permission to be expatriated, and of these only 64 had been granted. Does that fact not back up the evidence given by the Japanese during the Fisheries Commission which I have already quoted? I said there were two reasons. That is one of them. As regards the second, I will quote again from this pamphlet "Facts." Article 24 says:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding five articles-[DOT]
One of which I have already read.
A male person of the age of 17 and upwards can lose Japanese nationality only if he has already performed his service in the army or navy or if he is not bound to perform such service.
And there are very few of them who come under the category of not being bound to perform such seivice. As a matter of fact, they are so strict in that regard that any Japanese going home to Japan who stays there
Naturalization Acts

more than 30 days is likely to be corralled and made do his service. There is one exception. If he goes to get a wife for importation into the United States he is allowed 90 days. But if they did expatriate any of their nationals these Japanese would in all these cases be trained soldiers or sailors. Everyone would be a man who had gone through their course of training with all that it implies, not only military training but the essential Japanese education with all the high ideals they inculcate in their people about devotion to the emperor, who is their god, and to their nation.
Does that regulation with regard to military training apply even to Japanese born in the United States?

Certainly it applies. Article 20 provides that a Japanese subject who has acquired nationality in a foreign country by reason of his birth and domicile there may be expatriated with the permission of the Minister of State. But if he is over 17 he must undergo the military training of the Japanese, which is not the very best preparation for citizenship as a British or an American subject. In case that is not enough to prevent the Japanese being expatriated, there is another clause:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding six articles, a person who actually holds a civil or military position can lose his Japanese nationality only after he has lost his position.
That might be considered to apply only to diplomatic positions; but it can also very readily be applied to military positions, in this sense. Those of us who come from the Old Country know that there was a system under the militia there under which a man trained for a certain length of time. After he had put in so many years of service he was placed on the permanent reserve of the country. I do not know, but it is likely that some such system exists in Japan, because every nation that has compulsory military training invariably place its soldiers, after their term of service, on the reserve force. A man in Japan will be registered when in military service as No. so-and-so in such-and-such a regiment of infantry, and after he has completed his training it is very reasonable to suppose that he still remains on the books of the corps and therefore occupies a military position. Whether that is so or not, however, it certainly lends itself to such suggestion and is borne out by the fact I have already cited, that out of 90,000 Japanese born in America only 74 have applied for expatriation, of which number 64 were allowed to be expatriated.

So much for that phase of the question. I might also refer to the evidence prepared by the American Legion, which is a reliable and reputable body in the United States, which evidence was collected to be placed before congress. I won't quote it; I will merely give a summary of it. It appears from the evidence that there practically exists in the United States to-day, more particularly in California, government of the Japanese nation over their nationals in that state of the American union, which is above and superior or at least, extra to the laws of the United States. They have something practically corresponding to a state legislature which meets annually. The work is done by means of organizations. There is a big organization, and there are smaller ones that are tributary or subject to it in various districts, and certain elected members of these bodies meet once a year and pass regulations and so on. Then there is a higher body, something like the state Senate, which also meets annually in the same way. Under this system they levy a form of taxation upon their nationals. They do not call it by that term; they describe the tax as fees; but they have a regular system of taxing their nationals, who by means of membership fees are obliged to pay a certain sum to this Japanese government-for it cannot otherwise be described- which controls the Japanese nationals in the state of California. The nationals are also compelled by the laws which this governing body enacts to register all births, deaths and marriages, and even the movements of individual Japanese. If they move from one section of the state of California to another they are required to record the fact, not with the American authorities but with their own authorities in the state. They also have a precise system of education. The Japanese may go to all the white schools they choose, and as a matter of fact they do. But after hours they must attend their own Japanese school, where they are drilled in the very highest ideals of Japanese nationalism, certainly an excellent education for Japanese in Japan, but by no means a good preparation for either an American or a Canadian citizen.
Now, Sir, I should like to sum up this matter in two questions. Is it possible for a man to be loyal to two countries at once? And, secondly, is it right that he should be given an opportunity even to pretend to do so? It comes back to the old saying in the Bible, "Ye cannot serve two masters". It has been tried often enough, but it has never been successful.

I certainly would not accept the statement of the Japanese that he was forswearing his country because I do not believe he would be doing so. And another thing, our naturalization law does not require that. All our naturalization law requires is that the person becoming naturalized shall adhere to the country in which he is seeking adoption.

My question was this: If our law were such, would the hon. member accept the desire of the national rather than be bound by the laws of the country from which he came. If that were in our Naturalization Act, would he not think we should accept it? Over the other he has absolutely no control whatever.

Of course, this particular amendment does not deal with the naturalization of the Jap. It deals with cases where the minister can say, "Here is a man who is a subject of two nations at once. We will de-naturalize him." That question would have to be raised in the section of the act which naturalizes such a man, and it would be rather difficult to do because the position mentioned by the hon. gentleman would crop up. A Japanese would say "Yes, I have de-naturalized myself," and you would have no way of proving whether he had or had not. But this amendment only deals with those cases where a Jap, as an example, has pledged himself to be a subject true to Canada, and it is afterwards found that he is still adhering to the laws and jurisdiction of Japan. If he wishes under this to get out of that position, all he has to do is to apply to the government of his native country for a certificate of expatriation, which is the form required by the Japanese government. They call it a "declaration of losing nationality" or something of that kind. Let him produce that form showing his government had expatriated him, and then he would-

Is it not conceivable that the Japanese government might refuse him
that certificate despite his earnest desire to de-naturalize himself so far as his1 country of origin is concerned?

Yes, the Japanese government have been denying it at the rate of 60 to 90,000;- but I never yet met a Jap who would want to quarrel with his country over such denial-he would still be a Japanese. I would not worry myself as to his relations or his conscience all I would ask is: "Your government says; 'You cannot be. a Canadian citizen unless you are expatriated by permission from us. Very well go and get that permission from your government;, else you cannot remain a Canadian subject.'" That is the position I would take.
Going back to my original argument, which I had about completed, when it comes to a showdown under these conditions which I have outlined, where th^y are absolutely under the jurisdiction of their native country apparently of their owri. free will, I would say: There can be only one question as to which country they will adhere to; they will adhere to their own country, and naturalization, so far as Canada is concerned, will be a farce, and it is highly undesirable to perpetuate such a condition of things.

I may have misunderstood the hon. member, but I think he dropped the remark that we would not know whether the Jap had forsworn Japan or not. Of course, that forswearing could take place on Canadian soil.
"Mr. NEILL:	If he forswore himself until
he was black in the face he would still be a subject of Japan because he had not taken the only means of becoming expatriated and obtained a certificate of such expatriation from his native country. He might not be willing to remain a Japanese subject, but he would remain one nevertheless.

I understand that, but two courses were put forward by my hon. friend: whether we would exact a certificate of expatriation from the Jap's native government, or whether we "would be satisfied by his swearing away his allegiance to Japan in Canada. I understood the hon. member to say that we would not know whether the Jap had forsworn his allegiance to his country of origin or not. Of course we would know.

I say again that the only reason that I have asked for these amendments is to make the Naturalization Act passed by the government of my right hon. friend as workable as possible, to clothe it with as many safeguards as possible, and to facilitate the issue, without confusion or delay, of naturalization certificates to those entitled to them. I was not at all surprised when the suggestion was made that this is a very large power to place in one individual's hands; I grant it. The Naturalization Act and measures relating to immigration are always the subject of a great deal of controversy in this House. The matter of citizenship is a very important one, not only to those who apply for naturalization, but to those of us who are natural-born or naturalized British subjects. It is a question that should be very carefully studied, and it is my desire that the fullest consideration be given to the proposed amendments. This is not the first time that amendments to the Naturalization Act have been asked in this parliament. At the Imperial conferences of 1902, 1908 and 1911 the question was considered of adopting a uniform system of naturalization so that a man naturalized as a British subject in Canada or in the Old Country would lie a British subject in any part of the Empire, and finally that was arranged. I do not know that there is

Hon. A. B. Copp, Secretary of State, says that at present the judicial investigations are often so perfunctory and unsatisfactory that the department is obliged to make another investigation on its own account. Under the proposed plan the investigation would be made, presumably, by an official of the department. In theory it would be a strictly impartial investigation and the minister would decide each case on its merits alone. But past political experience has shown that it is not wise to depend too much on theories. In those parts of the country where the majority of the electors were friendly to the party in office there would be a very great temptation to the more zealous party supporters of the party

-particularly if an election were in prospect-to endeavour to influence the investigation or the action of the minister so as to deny, or postpone, the naturalization of persons who were believed to be not in favour of the government. That expresses my views more concisely and in better language than I am able to express them. I do not object to this proposal of the Secretary of State merely in a spirit of opposition; I do so because I honestly believe that it will be dangerous and not in accordance with what is right to place the power of naturalizing foreign-born subjects in the hands of any one minister, either now or at any future time.

The Secretary oi State (Mr. Copp) suggested a little time ago that it was very largely in the West that this matter had any considerable application. I think we ought to get away from the merely legal or technical side of 'the measure and consider the effect of the proposal on the large number of immigrants who are already in this country and others whom the government is seeking to bring here. There has been a tendency in the course of this discussion to regard the immigrants as being of a lower type intellectually than we are and as having lesser attainments along political lines than we have.
I do not think I heard that statement made in the House, this afternoon, anyway.

Further than that, there has been, at least on the part of some, a feeling that some of these immigrants may be possible criminals and that a very careful investigation ought to be made before they are granted citizenship. I would remind hon. members that a large number of our immigrants come to us from northern Europe and from the United States; that they are self-respecting, intelligent citizens, accustomed to a high standing of political life in their own country, and that they come here expecting to be granted similar rights and privileges in the country which they hope to make the land of their adoption. Under our existing law we ask them to wait for five years before they can be granted the full privileges of citizenship. I think that in regard to a very considerable number of immigrants that provision works a good deal of hardship. Five
years is a long time in our young and rapidly developing country for a man to be engaged in agriculture or in any other industry without having the privilege of a voice in the affairs of the country and in the making of its laws through the sending of their representatives to parliament. I would not say that those people who are more backward, who have no knowledge of our parliamentary institutions and perhaps but a slight knowledge of our language, should not be required to wait that length of time, but I would emphasize that five years is a long time to keep a great many prospective citizens waiting. Then, when they reach the end of that five years they find it extremely difficult, in some instances at least, to obtain their citizenship.
I think of one particular case of a gentleman in whose history I have been a little bit interested-and I am sure the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray) will bear me out; we were discussing this matter not very long ago-a gentleman who is a graduate of a Canadian university, who is spoken of in the very highest terms by the professors in that institution and yet who is unable to obtain his papers, because of the arbitrary decision of the Secretary of State. The gentleman to whom I refer occupies a position of responsibility with a reputable organization, yet, after a good many years in this country, after qualifying himself for a first class position by attendance at a university, he is unable to obtain the citizenship which Canada ought to grant to him. The Secretary of State suggests that he is responsible to this House in regard to his action, yet I take it rhat in practice it is extremely difficult for those of us who want to see that justice is done to these immigrants to have the decision changed when it comes to a particular case of this kind.
I would further like to call the attention of the committee to the relationship of this naturalization law to other laws on our statute books. For instance, we have an Immigration Act; and we are told that we do not need to worry very much about men who are liable to deportation, because if they stay in this country for five years they may become naturalized. They may; but on the other hand, if they are naturalized under present regulations which have existed for a considerable number of years, they may be denaturalized at the will of the Secretary of State. We talk about British citizenship being held in high repute, and I think we all in this House hope that that may be case. But the alien who is coming in here and is anxious to obtain Canadian citizenship cannot hold it as a very valuable thing when at the instance of one
Naturalization Acts

man he may be denaturalized and thereby lose all the rights and privileges which ought to come through the obtaining of Canadian citizenship. That is one of the points that comes up in connection with the Immigration Act; these two acts dovetail one into the other. So I would emphasize that the non-Canadian-bom immigrant who comes in here not only has no rights during the first five years of his residence, but may, even after be has been naturalized, have his rights taken away from him by arbitrary action.
Up to the present the arbitrary powers of the Secretary of .State have been largely confined to the taking away of naturalization, but by this proposed amendment he will have it in his power to refuse naturalization. Surely if we are really living in a democracy the friends and neighbours of the immigrants, those people of the same community ought to have the right to decide whether or not a man should obtain citizenship. In some debates on the floor of this House we have had the rights of the provinces very jealously guarded. I would like to think that the communities ought to be guarded so that people out in my own province, for instance, would have a perfect right to take into their fellowship those whom they think suitable for that citizenship. It might very readily be that the ideas of the people in my own city of Winnipeg or in my own province of Manitoba might differ from those of the people in Ottawa. I think then that we in Manitoba ought to decide who are the right and proper persons to be taken into the citizenship of Manitoba. I think it can be readily seen that some of the opinions at least of the residents of the province of British Columbia differ from those of the peoples in eastern Canada. Although I cannot agree with all the positions of the people of British Columbia I would say that to a very large extent the people of British Columbia ought to decide who are the right and proper persons to be taken into their citizenship. The whole thing ought not to be left, to the arbitrary power of the Secretary of State.
We have had a good deal said there with regard to the necessity of keeping out undesirables, of being very careful to safeguard the rights of citizenship. I agree with a good deal of that. On the other hand I would like to point out to you that we ought to be eager to admit to citizenship every worthy resident of Canada. We have had a good deal of talk in recent years about the necessity of bringing about reforms through constitutional means. I would suggest that if you do not enfranchise the people they [Mr. Woodsworth.J
have no opportunity of bringing about the reforms which they desire through constitutional means. I have been trying as best I can to represent one considerable section of this community, the Labour people, and I have found as I have gone in and out of a good many camps in northern Ontario, in Nova Scotia and away out in British Columbia that a very considerable proportion of the people who are engaged in the work of this country are without the opportunity of really doing anything through what we term constitutional means. The same thing is true of a very considerable number of people in the agricultural districts of the three prairie provinces. We say to them: Use the parliamentary machine; elect your members to parliament. I have been trying to say that to them, and they retort: We are without the vote; we do not find it possible for us to obtain the vote. Thus we are rapidly coming to the position where if this political franchise is not given men will be driven to take action along other lines. I would submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that whilst we try to safeguard the franchise, whilst we try to exercise reasonable precautions in admitting people to the citizenship of this country, there is another danger, and that is that wo make a very considerable number of the people of this country feel that it is hardly worth while. By making it too difficult we almost compel them to attempt to bring about what they desire in this country through means other than those which we call parliamentary.
I am not going to speak at length with regard to the centralization of the whole of this authority. I would join with others who have spoken on that and ask that the Secretary of State reconsider this whole matter.
I think it is for him to work out a scheme whereby people in the local districts would have a right to admit or reject people to their citizenship: We have the responsibility here of protesting against the centralization of all authority in the hands of one man. In Canada we are a great people of between eight and nine millions. We are throwing open our doors and saying that we hope to have hundreds of thousands of people take up their residence among us and ultimately become citizens of Canada. It seems absolutely absurd that we should say that one man out of the eight or nine millions of people in Canada is to have the absolute decision as to how many people and what people shall come in through the gate of citizenship and whether or not when they do come in they may be ejected at his will.

To refuse naturalization?
Not to refuse, but to say whether a man shall be admitted to naturalization.

My point was that he already has the power. At least upon his recommendation a man may be denaturalized. Here is the clause to which I referred:
Without prejudice to the foregoing provisions the Governor in Council shall by order revoke a certificate of naturalization granted by the Secretary of State of Canada under this act, or granted under any Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada in any case in which he is, upon the report of the Secretary of State of Canada, satisfied that the person to whom the certificate was granted, was
Among a number of other things,
not of good character at the date of the grant of the certificate.
There is nothing specific as to what is intended by good character. It simply means that if any man is obnoxious to the Secretary of State or indeed to the party in power at any particular time he may be declared to have been not of good character at the date of the granting of the certificate, and without any trial whatever the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Secretary of State may cancel his certificate of naturalization.

I rather took it that the major burden of the hon. gentleman's remarks was a complaint about the ungenerosity of our naturalization laws, and, perhaps inadvertently, he dropped remarks which could only mean that the power of the Secretary of State of denying naturalization had been enlarged by this change. If there is no misunderstanding it is entirely all right.

I did not intend
to say that the power technically or legally had been enlarged, but I do insist that by granting the Secretary of State such absolute arbitrary power the situation is materially affected. If he chooses so to do he can without any reference to the people of the community deny to large numbers of people the right to become citizens.

I had not intended to take any part in this discussion, but some remarks dropped by the Secretary of State cause me to do so. I think he is under a little misapprehension in regard to the difficulties of the process of securing citizenship. I have the honour to represent a constituency where there are a goodly number of foreigners and I would just like to point out this: Each one does not have to travel fifty or one hundred miles to lay his case before a district court judge. What is usually done is that an application is made by a number of foreigners. They usually live in groups in the country and they make application to the district court judge to hold a sitting in their midst. I am not so closely in touch wdth the working out of this plan that I am prepared to say that in no case has the judge refused, but I know of many cases where the judge has acceded to the request and has held the sitting in their midst. That enables them to reach the judge by travelling a distance of ten, twelve or fifteen miles or perhaps less. Such a procedure is comparatively easy. I was glad to hear the minister state that he did not think it wise to place unnecessary obstacles in the way .of applicants for naturalization. I cannot conceive of the reasoning which seeks to prove that a man is likely to become a better citizen if he is made to drive one hundred miles rather than ten or fifteen miles. I cannot see that an applicant is likely to experience a change of heart in the right direction by having to drive a longer distance. To have to drive a distance of one hundred miles and probably remain a couple of days from home is a handicap that should not be placed in the way of those endeavouring to obtain citizenship. I thoroughly approve of an examination to see that applicants are properly qualified, that they are inspired by high ideals, and that they are anxious to become good citizens.
The remarks of the minister touching 'the present system did not impress themselves strongly upon me. I have heard no objection to the present plan. It seems to me that an inquiry by a competent official comparatively near to the home of the applicant is a proper
Naturalization Acts

thing. The Canadian neighbours of applicants who have known them day in and day out perhaps for five years, perhaps for a longer period, are the proper persons to give information to the judge as to the kind of citizens they are likely to make.
I cannot agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Woodsworth) when he speaks of all these foreigners as coming to Canada with very high ideals of citizenship. From my experience- and I have come into contact with many of them-they have been imbued in their homeland with a fixed hatred of government control and of government institutions. They are ready to oppose anjdhing in the form of government, and it takes some little time for their minds to be disabused of that idea; it takes some little time for them to realize that they are living in a country where they can [DOT] enjoy greater freedom than they did in the countries from which they came. I do not think that a residence of five years in Canada is too long to insist upon. I would be very sorry to see the present arrangement changed because I fear there might be abuses just before election time. I would cast no reflection whatever upon the motives of the minister. I do not for a moment think that he would take advantage of the change that is proposed in the law in order to naturalize a goodly number of foreigners on the eve of an election. Nevertheless, I submit that at a time like this, when people are worked up to a white heat of excitement, there are persons, anxious to roll up as big a vote as possible, who would not hesitate at any means in order to get these foreigners naturalized. That might be done possibly without the minister's knowledge. I think that to require applications to be posted in the office of the clerk of the court for three months is a splendid safeguard and would prevent a great number of foreigners being naturalized just in time to cast their votes. I think we are far more likely to get a good class of citizens naturalized, and far more likely to weed out undesirables, when the naturalization proceedings take place some months before an election.
I have listened carefully to the discussion and I must say that I am in sympathy with the present system with, perhaps, some little modification. Personally I have not been able readily to see the difficulties complained of, -but if there are such I would be willing to agree to some slight modification to bring about an improvement; but the idea of centralizing these proceedings and giving so much power to one man does not meet with my sympathy.

I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) has about the right idea with regard to the Naturalization Act. I say that as one having had considerable experience under the old Naturalization Act, and under the present Naturalization Act passed in 1914. I was very glad indeed to hear the Secretary of State say that he was open to receive suggestions and to consider them. Such an attitude on the part of a minister leads to that serious consideration which a bill of this character merits, and I feel quite sure that he meant what he said in that respect. In view of the minister's statement I will try to add something to the suggestions already advanced. It is true that in 1914, when the present Naturalization Act was introduced members sitting on the same side of the House as the Secretary of State strongly opposed giving the minister the discretionary powers which he exercises under the act. Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself doubted the wisdom of giving so much discretion to the Secretary of State. In reply to his remarks Mr. Doherty, then Minister of Justice, said:
Of course if our position is that in Canada we can never produce any man to fill any position to whom discretion can be confined, tihen this is too wide a power to give to the Secretary of State, but, if it is a useful thing to this country that there should be a discretionary power, I would have to admit that we could not do it, because we never can get a Secretary of State who can be trusted to exercise his discretion about a matter of this sort.
I think Mr. Doherty was quite correct in his view. As I understand it, what is objected to now is not that the present discretionary power of the Secretary of State should be continued but that. discretionary power vested in the judges should be wiped out. I think that the provision of the act of 1914 requiring the applicant to appear personally before a judge for examination is a very necessary precaution. As was pointed out by the leader of the Opposition it does not follow, that because the judge gives a favourable certificate of recommendation the Secretary of State must of necessity grant the applicant naturalization; he does not have to do anything of the kind. There must, however, be a favourable report from
10 p.m. the judge before the applicant can be naturalized. I think it would be a mistake to wipe out the necessity of an examination before a judge. I may be mistaken, but I venture to say that the desire on the part of the department to make this change at the present time has arisen out of a course pursued by a certain judge in the province of British Columbia who in his wisdom-and very properly I think; I entire!''

commend him for what he did in the matter-in almost every instance refused to give a certificate of recommendation to Japanese applying to be naturalized as British subjects. The judge in question saw through their subterfuges, and notwithstanding the strong pressure which was brought to bear on him absolutely declined to recommend that Japanese be naturalized as British subjects. I do not think that altogether suited the officials of the Department of the Secretary of State. Consequently it may be for that reason they wish to obviate the necessity for the judicial examination. I think in most cases where the judges refuse to recommend naturalization they are acting on reasonable grounds and according to their best judgment.
I do not think that the delay of three months prescribed by the act is undesirable. A person must live in Canada for a considerable number of years before he is eligible to be naturalized. It is better that there should be a delay of three months in these naturalization cases rather Jthan that naturalization proceedings should be rushed through on the eve of an election. They should not want this citizenship merely to vote at a particular election. Citizenship carries with it a great deal more than that. They have been considering the matter and qualifying themselves for some years, so I do not think a period of three months is too long for the procedure.
I was struck with the remark made by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), when he said that he regretted seeing large bunches of naturalization certificates go through. Perhaps he has had the same experience as I have had in seeing large bunches of naturalization certificates go through. I have seen them go through by the hundreds up in the very	territoiy	that	the	Secretary	of State(Mr. Copp) referred to, the Yukon territory. In 1902, on the eve of an election, I have seer them go through by the hundreds, go through so fast that they did not take time to register them. I have seen them go through on the same date as the notices of application, whereas three weeks' notice was required. It was just a case of one, two, three, and out. I say in the	light	of	experience	that thenecessity for centralization of this power to naturalize is great, and that you should not distribute it over the country at large. If that centralization had been required in those days, that abuse could never have been perpetrated. At that time people were naturalized or allegedly naturalized, who, as a matter of fact, never became British subjects, and for years	they did not	find	out that	they hadbeen	duped.	That	was	due to a slipshod
Naturalization Act, taken advantage of by officials who knew better.
The Secretary of State would be well advised to consider the matter carefully before he wipes out the provision requiring that an applicant shall get a favourable recommendation from a county judge before he can have a certificate of naturalization. I for one do not object to having the final discretion vested in the Secretary of State; I think that is the proper official to exercise that discretion and to give final judgment; but great care should be taken in bringing the application up for his final decision. It would be a mistake to do away with the present necessity for a favourable certificate by a judge.

I do not
wish to reiterate arguments that have been advanced; but I want to state to the minister that I am one of those ordinary members to whom he refers, and whom he could excuse for having suspicions of his bill. The reasons I have suspicions of the power which this bill would confer on the Secretary of State are the same as those enunciated by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black). He referred to the year 1902. A little later than that, similar cases came under my observation in a district that I know very well, where natural-[DOT] ization certificates were issued, I am sure, byf the score, and I think I would be safe in using the same expression the hon. member did in his case, that hundreds were issued. I am not stating that the people who so secured their naturalization papers, were not, in the majority of cases, entitled to them. Probably they were; but I know in that rush a goodly number were not entitled to them, and the whole effect of that procedure was to cheapen, to lessen the intrinsic value of the citizenship so acquired.
I am in favour of some action being taken towards the end which, I think, the Secretary of State had in view when he prepared this bill, that is, to place this valuable acquirement of citizenship within the reach of those to whom it is due. It has been pointed out- and I think it should be emphasized-that a goodly number, probably the majority of those who will be applying for citizenship in this country in the next few years, will be those immigrants who have come to our shores, and who in the years prior to their application for citizenship, have been pioneers in our frontier settlements. The conditions which surround them should be taken into consideration, because the majority that this legislation will provide for will be such as those. If the conditions, the regulations, which are to surround our immigration policy are properly carried

out, those who come to our country in the next few years will be placed in what may be termed our frontier settlements; they will be pursuing agriculture. I have in mind at the present time a settlement within my constituency where there are, or were last fall, many people living who are entitled to citizenship so far as I understand the matter; that is, they have performed the necessary residence duties and other requirements. But because this would take at least four days, and that, providing that the court was prepared , to receive and consider their applications immediately on their arrival at the court, and because it would cost them a very considerable sum of money, they were unable to secure their citizenship papers. They had made application to have an officer or the judge himself come to them. I was glad to hear my colleague the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) state that he knew of cases where judges, by coming to settlements like that, had made it possible for such people to secure their citizenship papers. I do not know of any such case, and it was stated to me by a judge of my province that he had no authority to hold sittings outside of those places appointed in the calendar, and that he could not come to those who so requested. The people in the settlement to which I refer were willing to pay all the expenses of the judge or any deputy or officer he would appoint to come to them. That would be a small thing compared with the combined expenses of the whole settlement in going for their naturalization papers. That is only one instance in many, and in a case like that some action is necessary along the line which the. minister, I think, had in mind when he drafted this bill.
But I am afraid in the terms of the bill as he has presented it to us, he did not properly safeguard the giving of citizenship rights. I feel that that should be safeguarded, and there are ways of doing so. The Secretary of State, in making his remarks to-night, rather discredited or discounted the value of posting in post offices notices of application for citizenship. I can fully understand, in the example he gave and similar examples, where that is of little value. In a post office in a city or a large town, that probably would not be a good way of giving publicity to the fact that individuals were applying for citizenship rights. But, perhaps, the minister and many hon. members can understand that in rural post offices these notices do receive attention, for the very reason that I argued just a moment ago that that is where most of these would and should be posted under the cases (Mr. C. W. Stewart.]
that this legislation would be providing for in the . next few years, I want to give a concrete instance of this. Just a few years ago, a short time ago, in a rural post office, notices of application for citizenship were posted by a number of persons whb, under the law which at present exists, were not entitled to apply for citizenship. They were of enemy alien extraction in nationality; but by giving a wrong birthplace on their application to the clerk of the court, they thought to overcome that difficulty and to secure the right of citizenship. Their applications were posted in the rural post office, and because they came from a settlement where many others knew them intimately, having come from the old country with them, this point received attention; notice was given to the clerk of the court, and those persons who so made application did not wrongfully receive their citizenship rights at that time.
In all cases where rural conditions exist, those who know best the qualifications of applicants for citizenship are the people of the district and those who are or have been neighbours of the persons applying. I would suggest then that this provision should not be done away with. Whether it should go to the judge of the court or whether the Secretary of State should have the privileges and judicial rights of the judge in that respect, I am not at all particular.
But I do say that at least sufficient notice should be given in the district or the municipality in which the application is made, so that those who know intimately the history and the immediate past of the persons so applying may have an opportunity, just as is provided in the old act, of filing in the court opposition to the application, stating the ground on which they base that opposition. If that provision had been embodied in the bill I think I would have supported the minister and favoured the bill as he brought it down. But because I feel he has not placed sufficient safeguards around the granting of naturalization I am opposed to the measure. I believe that if this bill were to be made law and to be put into force the conditions would be very similar to those that existed previous to 1914, and I am sure that a number of hon. members in this House know what those conditions were in certain districts at that time, at least in the West.

I want to say a few words in support of the minister and I shall do so for the reason that as I have observed the process of our naturalization law in the province of British Columbia, it has not functioned properly. I do not agree with the

suggestion that has been made that the minister is seeking to have this bill passed in order to use it in any arbitrary or partisan way. I disagree entirely with the remarks of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) in which he suggests that the minister is more or less anxious to have the bill passed so that he may be able to facilitate the granting of naturalization to orientals. It is in regard to the naturalization of orientals that I desire to speak briefly. I have found, in my expe-lience in British Columbia, that there has never yet been any objection to any application for naturalization. What is everybody's business is apparently nobody's business. The application forms are posted up at the usual place, but no one takes any notice of them. They go through a certain process and are finally approved of; but I never yet knew of anyone protesting their acceptance. Some time ago in British Columbia in connection with the fishing regulations legislation was passed providing that no fishing licenses should be issued to any man who was not a British subject either by birth or by naturalization. That was believed to be the proper means of preventing orientals from taking part in the fishing industry. But we found almost instantly that orientals were being naturalized wholesale. I am thoroughly in sympathy with the minister's bill, for this reason, that we shall be able to fix the responsibility in this matter. Up to the present time we have never been able to determine just who was responsible for the wholsale granting of naturalization papers to orientals. I was present at a meeting in the city of Prince Rupert at which a man directly interested in the fishing industry made a significant remark. He said, "You expect to prohibit, from fishing, people, who are not British subjects. Let me tell you that all the fishermen on the Skeena river are British subjects; and I will tell you more than that. There were 75 of them naturalized in your own town last summer and no one knew anything about it". The member for Yukon makes the suggestion that the minister is endeavouring to override the expressed opinion of one of the judges in the city of Vancouver. Well, I am supporting the minister in this bill because I want to determine just who is responsible for the issuing of papers, and I shall be able under this legislation to know who is responsible for granting naturalization to people who should not be naturalized. There is one other point. I find that when any man desires to become naturalized the usual method is to appear before a lawyer, at least in British Columbia; and the standard fee in the section of the country from which I come is $25 for the legal work in connection therewith.
I do not regard this bill as an autocratic move on the part of the government or an attempt to secure autocratic powers by the minister. Rather, I consider it to be the embodiment of the principle of responsible government. Someone, has to be responsible for the granting of naturalization papers, and if you are going to have responsible government you must make the proper minister answerable for his actions. If we do that we shall be able to determine just exactly where the fault lies when papers are issued to persons who are not entitled to them.
