I do not know whether I was wrong, but certain changes have taken place in the complexion of the House which incline me to take another view, because when I was then talking against the same question now before the House the Secretary of State was an entirely different person from the Secretary of State to-day. So that conditions are not quite the same. I remember trying to wax eloquent when I pointed out thq danger to which the public might be exposed were we to put into the hands of the Secretary of State this power of granting or withholding certificates of naturalization, involving as it did the franchise, particularly on the eve of a general election. But it was stated at the time, I think by the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who was in charge of the bill on that occasion, that the Secretary of State or some person representing the government would have to be a party to the granting of naturalization certificates, inasmuch as the bill came to us from England. The bill had to be fashioned on the English act, and it was indicated that the administration had to be a party to legislation of this kind, and to the granting of certificates of imperial naturalization. We were therefore limited to the discussion of the entire question. The government said at the time, "Unless you take this you cannot have Imperial naturalization."
I do not know whether it is generally known to this committee that previous to 1914 we had a naturalization law which conferred upon the applicant merely a limited form of na-
Naturalization Acts

turalization, or one that declared that the applicant was to be a British subject within the Dominion of Canada and not elsewhere. By the new act of 1914 and its amendments, Imperial naturalization was granted to applicants and we abolished the restricted or purely Canadian form of naturalization. Consequently we had to conform to the rules insisted upon by the British government. I understand that under the British system it is not necessary that the judicial authorities should in any way be parties to the granting of certificates of naturalization. It is purely a matter of state, for the administration. Involving citizenship and franchise, it was declared to be a matter not within the purview of the judicial authorities but merely one for the Secretary of State or some other member of the administration.
At present we have dual systems working together; we have the judicial and we have the executive. As was very well pointed out to-day, the Secretary of State has some responsibility; if any abuses arise under his department in regard to granting naturalization they can be brought before the House and before the country, they can be made the subject of discussion on the hustings, and consequently the Secretary of State, no matter how favourable he may be to his own party would have to go rather gingerly and refrain from doing anything which the law declared he should not do. The Under Secretary of State, who has charge of these matters reports that the present system is altogether unworkable, that it is cumbersome and useless, and he asks for a change. Now, the Secretary of State himself says he is not particularly wedded to this proposed section.
Is it not absolutely necessary in order to carry out the convention between the Imperial government and the colonies-
The dominions.
-and the dominions, yes, that we follow the lead given us in the Imperial legislation which takes away the power of granting naturalization from the judiciary and gives it to the executive?

That, I understand, is the rule in England. But we have attempted to be more careful and surrounded naturalization with more safeguards. Consequently we introduced the judiciary into the question. It seems to me that the Department of State can make exactly the same investigations as the judge does under the present system. I know something about how these petitions for naturalization are granted. Application is

made by an attorney on behalf of the person desiring naturalization. Before decision is given by the judge an investigation is conducted-in the city of Montreal it is conducted by the Mounted Police, why I do not know, except that I suppose being a federal police force it is their duty to do that class of work. After the Mounted Police have investigated and reported that the applicant is a fit and proper person to be granted a certificate of naturalization, the judge in turn reports to the Department of State. Now, the Mounted Police might just as well report to the Department of State direct without the intervention of the court at all, and inasmuch as it is stated that the system at present is, as I said before, cumbersome and unworkable I would agree to the change suggested by the Secretary of State. Of course, if any other easier and more workable system can be suggested I am prepared to consider it and perhaps to vote for it. The Secretary of State has said that he is open to suggestions.

In the hon. member's opinion, whatever procedure is to be followed, whether a judicial, a police or any other sort of investigation, ought it not be set out in the act instead of being a matter of regulation?
I fancy the proposed bill is based pretty much upon the English practice
*It is an exact copy in section 25.

If it works well in England why should it not work equally well here? My hon. friend should be the very last person to oppose any English system, because he insists that nothing good can come out of any place except England.
Who?
And perhaps I ought to add New Brunswick.
I do not take that view. Very many good things come out of Quebec, you know, including my hon. friend.
Hear, hear.

And very many good things go in from Quebec. I would point out to the committee that we must be careful in making changes in this law because we may find ourselves outside the privilege given us by the British government on Imperial naturalization. We have to follow certain well defined rules to secure such naturalization.

Then at that rate we must have been outside for some years.

No, I am referring to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I venture to say that his amendment would not be acceptable to the British government, and if passed it would probably result in the denial to us of Imperial naturalization, which we value bo highly. It will be remembered that in 1911 Sir Wilfrid Laurier brought this matter up at the Imperial Conference at London. There had been an agitation for Imperial naturalization. It was the subject of discussion on many occasions, but in 1911 we were told that such naturalization would be granted on our conforming to certain rules. Previous to that time three years was the time prescribed by us for naturalization. The Imperial government insisted upon five years' domicile. We conformed to that requirement. We conformed also in the matter of having the certificate issued by the Secretary of State. Now, as I understand it, under the English system we do not require the intervention of courts of justice at all, and inasmuch as there is practically no danger so long as a good Liberal administration is in power that the act will be in any way abused by the Secretary of State, I would be in favour of seeing that the Secretary of State obtained the powers asked for, with the proviso of course of voting to amend the bill as soon as the opposition comes into power.

Mr. Chairman, I am
frank to say that I do not find myself in full accord with the minister with regard to section 4 of his bill. I think the question can be considered from two points of view: first, that of protection of the country; second, that of the applicant for naturalization. As the Naturalization Act stands at present the country has twofold protection: the person desiring naturalization is required to apply personally to a judge, and the minister acting as an appellate court must review the decision of the judge. In that way the country is amply protected.
Now, naturalization is a very valuable right. It has long been settled in civilized countries that the judicial function should be kept entirely separate from the executive. And in dealing with the rights of citizenship the judicial function should exercise a very large and paramount jurisdiction. In this case we have now a court of appeal. We have many judges deciding upon applications for naturalization, ' 157
and in this way we have a general view of the many judicial minds. There is a marked danger of turning this wide judicial operation into a perfunctory act by a mere department of the state. What does the proposed change involve?
It is to be an inquiry by the police forces into the character of the applicant, and a report by them direct to the minister. The minister, sitting in appeal, does not see the applicant and has no opportunity of personally examining the policeman. He does not know the mental calibre of the man who is reporting; he knows nothing, except by letter or affidavit, of the man who is making the application. He proposes to extend that very unsatisfactory condition to first hand ab initio examination of all those who report. We can take the case of the average policeman, untrained in investigation, perhaps more or less prejudiced, reporting adversely in respect to the application of an individual possessed of splendid qualifications for citizenship. Like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) I think the judge who is familiar with the local situation, familiar with the calibre and character of the applicants in that locality, is by all means best qualified to decide in the matter. I do not like to see * a matter of such vital importance to the individual dealt with merely by a department of the state, it is a question that should come within the scope of judicial inquiry, and I think it ought so to remain.
Surely an administration that nominates the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada ought to be trusted to grant a certificate of naturalization of an applicant?
But the judges after that cannot vote, while the man after he is naturalized, can.
Therefore the man who can vote has more power than a judge who is on the bench.
Not more power, no.

The difference is this: In the one case there is no interest in the matter at all but that of doing what is right. In my opinion it is better, rather than to put it under the control of one person, to have the benefit of a variety of views, those of the judges all over the land. I say that the matter is too vital and of too much importance to become a mere matter of departmental administration. *

It is evident from this discussion itself, and it should be reassuring, that the Secretary of State will, if this pro-

Naturalization Acts

posal is adopted, exercise merely the same powers and the same functions he is exercising now. We have the evidence that the work of the judges has been, not universally but in a substantial number of cases, so unsatisfactory that the department has ignored the report of the judges. I am not at all certain, with due respect to what I would call the eminent authority on the other side-and I say "eminent authority" in all sincerity-that the Secretary of State has not power affirmatively to naturalize a man against whom a judge has reported on regular application. I see some reason why he should have that power. I will suppose, if he had that power, that it was to cover what I might call emergent cases or special circumstances. For instance, a judge might in all honesty make a report against an applicant, and it might turn out within a short time that only those appeared against him who were malicious and spiteful and who had fabricated evidence to do him harm. That judge might die; there might be no circuit there for months. Would it not be feasible to get the facts before the Secretary of State, to show that there had been that miscarriage of justice, and let him exercise his own discretion in the matter? One could cite cases indefinitely where it might well be the prerogative of the Secretary of State to step in and grant naturalization to a man against whom the judge had technically shut the door. He might be a man who had been here five years, who was known to be an outstanding friend of Canada, yet the court might not meet in time to grant his naturalization before the occurrence of some event in connection with which he could be of some great national service. For instance, we might want to make him a delegate to some international convention. These are conceivable cases, and they are not to be sneered at merely because the man of my illustration has not up to that time been a naturalized Canadian citizen.
I could multiply illustrations well within the realm of reason to show that it is only just and sensible that the Secretary of State should have that supreme power. The right hon. leader of the Opposition rather thought that the Secretary of State should have come here armed with an opinion from the Justice department one way or the other. I would rather say that the burden was the other way. There is a clause in the act which on its face does seem to give the Secretary of State that power, and I should say that the man who disputes it should himself come here armed with an authoritative deliverance to convince us that the clause does not mean what it seems to say. rM. Putnam.]
Hon. gentlemen opposite practically admit that a substantial proportion of the judges have been doing their work in a slipshod way, and the moment they admit that they admit that the present system falls down. Simply because some judges do their work in a painstaking and a thorough mann/er does not enable us to say that the system is a success; I would say that if three per cent of the judges go wrong the system is a failure, particularly if naturalization is as sacred a thing as hon. members opposite in both groups have insisted this afternoon and this evening. If we give the Secretary of State these powers we give him work to do to which his department greatly to its credit, is already enured. The evidence is that the judges were not doing the work; the depart- [DOT] ment has had the power to grant a certificate when the judge reported adversely to the application-and they have been using an emergent power as a general power, due to the lack of thoroughness and the lack of painstaking care on the part of the judges. My own experience in this matter is limited, but it is sufficient to give you an illustration of how slipshod the method is in my experience. The application is filed and the notice is posted. Nobody reads it. I consider that a former speaker to-night was happy in the expression: "What is everybody's business is nobody's business." The judge perfunctorily says, "I will leave this until the last day of the term." and if no objection is registered it then goes through as a matter of course.
I do not for a moment impugn the integrity of the judge, but I do say he was not properly vigilant, and it is evident that a large proportion of the judges have not exercised the vigilance that they should. And when a considerable number of the judges were slack in their work, the minister very naturally took it for granted that he could not depend upon the reports of any of these judges in so critical a matter as that of naturalization.

I do not propose to delay the committee at any length but I would like very briefly to refer at the outset to the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), which has not been discussed. The amendment, as I understand it, calls for the prohibition of the granting of naturalization to any alien whose nationality in the country of origin is not revoked by that country itself. If the hon. member had included in his amendment a provision that such an applicant should be granted naturalization if he were himself willing tq forswear his former allegiance I think I could support it, but I do not think that this House should

Naturalization Acts
accept any suggestion to keep fastened the shackles of a foreign country upon any man who has lived in this land for five years, has proved himself a worthy citizen and desires to obtain naturalization. That is all I have to say on that. I do not think the commit-, tee should have very much difficulty in rejecting the amendment of the hon. member in the way in which it is framed.
Would the hon. gentleman object to my correcting him as to what the amendment is?
I would prefer to get the correction from the hon. gentleman who moved it.

As I understand it, the amendment does not apply to the case of application for naturalization at all, but applies later on, giving the Secretary of State power to denaturalize a person who has obtained naturalization under certain circumstances.

As I understand it, the
amendment calls for the denial of naturalization to men who have naturalization in other countries. Is that correct?

No, that is not the purpose of the amendment at all. The amendment is to deal with the case where a man has been naturalized in Canada, and as the hon. member says probably put in three years perhaps five or ten years ago and it is found to-day that he is still a subject of Japan obeying its laws, carrying out its customs, and giving adherence to Japan, when all he has to do to purge himself of that obligation is to apply to Japan to obtain a certificate of expatriation. If he cannot get that certificate of expatriation he is still a Japanese subject. He may want to get it; perhaps he is unfortunate, I do not know about that; but if he fails to get it or fails to apply for it he is certainly still a Japanese subject as well as being a Canadian subject, and if the hon. gentleman wants a test of the sincerity and the genuineness of these denaturalized Japanese in seeking to affiliate themselves to Japan he has only to look to the United States where out of 90,000 eligible only 74 applied for the certificate of expatriation from their native country, and only 64 applications were granted. But of 90,000 only 74 or 75 ever sought for it.
As the hon. member for New Westminster has said, this has nothing to do whatever with the merit or demerit of granting or refusing naturalization to a Jap or anybody else. It deals with the case where a man has been pretending to be a subject of Canada and it
is found years and years afterwards that he has been giving the most definite form of adherence to a foreign state.

If he is still giving definite adherence to his former state I am quite in sympathy with what the hon. member says. I think the result of the amendment if adopted would be exactly as I have indicated. It would rob a man who has obtained naturalization of his British citizenship. If the man himself cannot obtain release from the country of his former allegiance, even though he may be entirely willing and desirous of being a British subject only, he is deprived of his British citizenship. I object to that.
I have given an instance of their willingness to debar themselves by citing the United States where out of 90,000 eligible to do so only 74 applied for expatriation.

Would the hon. gentleman answer this? If the man in question who has already been naturalized in Canada asks from the country of his former allegiance a release from his former obligation and is refused, and if he is willing to disavow himself of allegiance to his former country, would the hon. member deprive him of Canadian citizenship?
No.

No, I would object to that. I wish to speak for a few moments on a matter that has been the subject of more serious debate, the matter of the mode of procedure for the obtaining of naturalization in this, country. We have the two views. We have the present method whereby the application for naturalization goes to the judge and if approved by him, to the Secretary of State, who again may reject or approve as he sees fit. We have on the other hand, the suggestion made in the present bill that the application instead of going to the judge should go direct to the Secretary of State and be decided there without any intervention by the judge. I am free to say that when the suggestion was first made that the method of procedure should be changed I felt that it was not a step in the right direction. I thought that the judge should perhaps be the best judge as to the qualifications of the applicant for naturalization, he being on the spot, perhaps being personally acquainted with the applicant and having a more intimate knowledge than would be possible to the officials at Ottawa or even to anyone they might send out to make the investigation. But I have discussed the matter fairly well with some of the officials, with those who know, and I am led to believe that it is pretty much a matter of theory which
Naturalization Acts

does not work out in practice, just as some of us believe very strongly in certain theories, say free trade, which we know in actual practice cannot exactly work out in any country.
Order.

I do not wish to be misunderstood by my Progressive friends. Perhaps I gave a very unfortunate example, and I do not want them to read into it anything that I did not intend. But the principle is still true. You can carry a theory to the extreme and find that it does not work out ic practice.
I for one am not one of those who would like to place an autocratic power in the hands of any official or of any member of the government and a power which he might abuse at certain times especially during an election. The only fair way and the only reasonable way, it seems to me, for the committee to arrive at a conclusion on the matter is to carefully compare in a practical way the exact results of the application of the two methods. I have outlined the first practice, the practice now in vogue, and the statement is made by those who know that the judges in their investigations of the applications of those who desire to become Canadian citizens are in so many words inefficient in the carrying out of .their duties.
(Now I do not care to make the charge that The judges in general throughout Canada do not properly investigate the qualifications of '*the various applicants for naturalization. I would not like to think they were all derelict in their duty, but I do know this, that there are cases where the judges who ought to know the law do not know the law with regard to naturalization, and when an applicant is rejected because of a lack of knowledge of the law I say that an injustice is done to him which ought not to be continued if we have any way of avoiding it. I know, for example, that a judge granted applications for naturalization although the law distinctly stated that the applicant did not have cer-tan qualifications. He approved of the applications. They were forwarded to Ottawa to the Secretary of State and there they were rejected. All that expense and delay could not have occurred if the application had gone in the first place to the Secretary of State. He at least knows the law and the various amendments that are made from time to time. I have known other judges who have accepted illiterates and who have rejected men on account of their racial origin, which under the law they were not entitled to do.

I take pretty well the opinion of the men who have been in charge of this work; I do not think there is any member here who is well qualified to judge as to the merits of the question. I am not so very much concerned as to the probability that the Secretary of State-as the member of a partisan government if you like-is going to abuse his power. I would not even like to say that I would be very suspicious of the Secretary	of State	of any other government which might have come into power -if it were a government led by the present leader of the Opposition, or a government led by the leader of the Progressive party. I am free to say that I have a little more confidence in the integrity and good faith of the public men of Canada. And even if they were inclined to be derelict in their duty it would mean that they would have to have the collusion of the men who are, if I may say so, the paid servants of the people of Canada-the deputy minister, the under secretary of state, and all the other officials; and any secretary of state who would dare, just prior to an election, to issue wholesale certificates of naturalization to aliens who he thought would vote for the party which he represented would find, I think, it would not be a very paying thing to do. He would find that his government and his party were responsible and I believe it would do him a great deal more harm than good.
We should not shrink very much from placing the power which is proposed to be given in the hands of the Secretary of State, because after all he is the responsible minister of a government, and if the people of this country have placed upon him responsibility and power it is right that he should exercise it, and if he does not live up to his duty punish him when next he appears before the electors. There are certain safeguards provided even now. In the first place when the application goes in it must be supported by the opinions of two reputable men in the community from which the applicant comes. In the second place if it is found that naturalization is granted to a man who is not worthy of it the Secretary of State and the government have the power to revoke that naturalization.
Now, we will say that a general election is upon us because it seems to be the fear of those who are in opposition that when a general election is impending the government in power, will naturalize those whom they believe are favourable to themselves, and perhaps withhold naturalization from those who are opposed ot them. As I say I do not believe there is very much likelihood of their

Naturalization Acts
doing that but they can do it at the present time. We will say there are two candidates. One is Conservative and the other is Liberal, and they come along with perhaps one or two hundred names of men whom they desire to see naturalized. We will say that a Liberal government is in power as is the case just now. The Liberal gets his men naturalized. The Conservative cannot get his men naturalized at all if the Secretary of State-

Can they be naturalized
without the three months elapsing? Must not the notices be posted up for three months?

Yes, but surely it is pretty
well known longer than three months in advance that a general election is pending, although not always. But this is true: Even throughout the whole term of parliament with a certain government in power the Secretary of State, if he were so inclined, could reject every application for naturalization from persons he thought were politically opposed to him I think it is entirely unlikely that such would be the case.
I am not very strong in my opinion with regard to this matter. I believe that the officials of the department of the Secretary of State are. entirely honest in the attitude they have taken, that their desire is to serve the public interest. I believe that the safeguards which would surround the whole situation in case the bill is adopted are ample and are quite sufficient in the interest of the country. It is for that reason that I feel, while supporting the bill as it stands at present, that if some other suggestion could be made that would satisfy the objections of those who are opposed, I would be very glad. I would like to see useful suggestions advanced rather than mere criticisms. To say that we must adhere to the old method is really not intelligent argument. If there are suggestions calculated to effect improvement I think hon. gentlemen opposite should make them, because the Secretary of State has intimated that he is willing to consider suggestions. As to the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni I feel that the committee ought to reject it.

What I say is, that the Secretary of State should have the advantage of the judge's report as well. As regards the refusal by the British Columbia judge to naturalize Japanese. Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 144, to amend the Radiotelegraph Act.
I think the minister should explain "what the law is and how this bill changes it.

Explanations were given when the resolution which preceded this bill was considered in committee, but I have no objection to repeat what was then said. Section 10 of the Radiotelegraph Act gives the Governor in Council the right to prescribe a tariff of fees to be paid for licenses and for examination for certificates of proficiency held and issued under the provision of this act. The aim of the bill is to add a certain paragraph for the purpose of authorizing the payment of a portion of that license fee to a provincial government or a private company for services given in connection with the operation of broadcasting stations and for services performed for the minister in connection with the licensing and inspection of stations.
Within the last two years radiotelegraphy has made considerable progress. Last year there were 10,000 licenses in Canada, and this year it is estimated that 50,000 licenses will be issued. Those licenses are mainly, almost ex-
Radiotelegraph Act

elusively, for receiving apparatus. Last year sixty-three licenses were issued for broadcast transmitting stations, but only forty were operated. This year only twenty-five licenses had been renewed. Those stations divide themselves into stations operated by big firms selling receiving apparatus, stations operated by newspapers for their advertisement, and then there are also broadcasting stations operated by provinical governments or private companies. The cost of establishing and maintaining a broadcasting station is rather high. The establishment may cost from $7,000 to $20,000, and the cost of upkeep is from $2,000 to several thousand dollars a year. Therefore, it is rather expensive, and many of the present broadcasting stations are going to discontinue.
This bill is to meet specially the situation in Manitoba, where there were two broadcasting stations, one operated by the Free Press and the other by the Tribune Both have been abandoned on account of the cost. The provincial government operates the telephone system in that province, and it is quite prepared to operate a broadcasting station, but it wants to have something in return. We think it is only fair that the thousands of persons who are getting enjoyment out of their receiving apparatus should pay something to the broadcasting station that supplies the enjoyment, and the idea is to give part of the license fee to the provincial government or to any company that will operate a broadcasting station. The licenses might be collected by the province itself, part of the license to be kept by the province for the cost of operating the broadcasting station and for the cost of collecting the licenses, and the other share to come to the federal government. This is the system in force in England. In England the cost of a receiving license is $2.50, $1.25 of which goes to the government and $1.25 to the broadcasting company. So far the license fee in Canada for receiving stations has been only $1. It is est'mated that about 50,000 licenses will be issued this year, so that would give an amount of $50,000. The cost of a license for a broadcasting station is $50.
When this legislation was in committee on the resolution, the former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) wanted to know the expenditure and the revenue last year The revenue received on account of license fees last year up to the 31st March amounted to $16,200. The cost of inspection service, including administration expenses at Ottawa, amounted to $19,250.18, and the cost of issuing licenses was $5,522.80, making a total of

$24,772.98. It must be noted that part of that cost of inspection goes for the inspection of the 160 commercial and eight navigation stations, the 255 Canadian ship stations and all foreign ships visiting Canadian ports carrying Canadian passengers, and this inspection would have to be made in any event. The estimated expenditure for the present year is:
Inspection service	 $24,920
Issue of licenses	 6,100
Total	 $31,020
The estimated revenue from license fees is approximately $50,000. This bill is for the purpose of giving to the Governot in Council power to make arrangements with a provincial government or any responsible government to broadcast and to keep part of the license fees for doing that service.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.

, Mr. RYCKMAN: Why should the whole cost of issuing licenses run into something like $5,000 or $6,000? What is the special expense in connection with issuing licenses?

In the large cities, Montreal, Toronto, even Quebec, there are officers specially employed for that purpose. In Montreal, last month, the first month of the present fiscal year, over 3,000 licenses have been issued. A special service is required for that work.

It has always been under federal jurisdiction.
I do not deny that. I see the bill was passed in 1913.
It is similar to the telegraph. It is interprovincial; it is national; it is even international. We have conventions with other countries.
